# Preface.

Reader, you who fulfill your duties toward God, toward the state, toward your neighbor, and toward yourself solely because <term>Christianity</term> <note>original: "Christenthum"</note> commands you to do so: I beg of you, set this book aside at first glance. Do not say: "Ha! You only make me curious; I must read it!" Believe me, you will lose your <term>peace of soul</term> <note>original: "Seelenruhe"; a state of spiritual and mental tranquility</note> over it, and I shall then wash my hands in innocence, for I have told you so beforehand. If you still refuse to take this advice, then read the Appendix as well, and read it again. Study it, and grasp it entirely, if you have the strength for it. Then you will find your peace of soul once more, and you will fulfill all duties toward God, toward the state, toward your neighbor, and toward yourself with double the joy.

I divide the thinking and reading public, in regard to my book, into three classes. To the first, I reckon those who search for truth with an unbiased mind and accept it, whether it has long been recognized or only recently discovered. I say, to this class I reckon all those who set themselves above the <term>prejudice</term> <note>The author refers here to the "Vorurtheil" of tradition—the habit of believing things simply because they are old or widely accepted.</note> that opinions and doctrines should be true merely because they have been considered established truths by many for millennia. To the second, I count those who praise <term>Voltaire</term> <note>François-Marie Arouet (1694–1778), a leading figure of the French Enlightenment known for his criticism of organized religion.</note> and his like as genuine lights of the world, and about things,

<summary>The author opens with a provocative warning that his book may challenge the reader's religious foundation, suggesting that only a thorough study of the appendix can restore one's peace of mind. He begins to categorize his audience, distinguishing between those who seek truth without prejudice and those who follow Enlightenment skeptics like Voltaire.</summary>
<keywords>preface, religious duty, peace of soul, Enlightenment, truth, prejudice, Voltaire, skepticism</keywords>

To the third class, I finally count those who teach the people and have taken an <term>official oath</term> <note>original: "Amtseid"; specifically referring to the oaths of orthodoxy taken by clergy or professors to uphold specific church doctrines</note> that they will always represent the opinions of the <term>Church Fathers</term> <note>The influential early Christian theologians whose writings established traditional orthodoxy</note> as divine truths, even if they should doubt one or the other of them.

My book cannot harm readers of the first class; rather, it must be of use to them, because they will grant me that I have sought the truth. They find in the traditional systems of <term>popular religions</term> <note>original: "Volksreligionen"; referring to the established, institutionalized faiths of the common people as opposed to a "natural religion" based on reason</note> various dogmas that contradict not only reason but also each other, often directly. God is, as almost every religion teaches, most perfect in all His attributes. But to the highest perfection belongs no suffering. Nevertheless, God is said to have taken on a human body and suffered on earth for mankind, merely to satisfy His own justice. Now, however, there are infinitely many <term>globes</term> <note>original: "Erdkugeln"; the author is referencing the Enlightenment-era scientific belief in the "plurality of worlds," suggesting that other planets are inhabited by rational beings</note>, on all of which surely creatures similar to humans dwell, who without doubt are not quite perfect, not quite without <term>sin</term>, just as we are—otherwise they would have to be equal to God, that is, God Himself in the literal sense. Should God then go from one world, from one globe to another, to [save] all...

Thus he wavers anxiously over terrifying abysses of agonizing doubts of death and life to the left and to the right, like a reed that the wind bends now to this side, now to that, threatening to break it at any moment. Thus I too wavered in mortal fears, and nothing could protect me from the fall but God by means of my reason. At least I believe I know for certain that I now stand firm. Should I still waver, still err, I ask for kind and thorough instruction; for I seek only truth, because without it I cannot be happy.

Readers of the second class will also find in my book no poison, but rather healing medicines for their sick insights, if they read it with deliberation and with a love for the truth. **Voltaire** <note>François-Marie Arouet (1694–1778), the French Enlightenment philosopher famous for his wit and attacks on organized religion</note> has made them into mockers of old traditions and doctrines: here they find no mockery, but rather serious searching for truth; at the very least, they must not take those passages that perhaps sound harsh or mocking in a mocking sense. It is not at all necessary to mock the artificial weaving of the old prophetic and mystery-philosophy, but merely to investigate from where the material for it was taken, and how it was woven together. **Voltaire** has made them mockers of immortality:

Now, something more must be said regarding the various treatises that appear in this book.

It is well-known that many passages of the Bible, but especially the imagery of the **Apocalypse** <note>the Book of Revelation</note>, cloud the minds of many people and even incite crimes. **Rosenfeld** <note>Hans Peter Rosenfeld (1732–1803), a self-proclaimed messiah in Prussia who led a small sect and was eventually imprisoned</note> and his followers use the **Prophets** and the **Revelation of John** to justify their crimes. Detailed accounts of this can be found in the first volume of the *Berlin New Monthly Journal* <note>original: "berlinischen neuen Monatsschrift", a leading publication of the German Enlightenment</note>. 

The **Moravian**-reborn shepherd <note>referring to the *Herrnhuter* or Moravian Brethren, a Pietist Christian movement known for emotional devotion</note>—who did not believe he was perfectly reborn or fully faithful unless he could sacrifice his most beloved, just as **Abraham** did—prayed to God for this cruel faith until he felt faithful enough to strike his three young sons dead with an axe and offer them as a sacrifice to God as a seal of his faith. This can be read in the first volume of the *Yearbooks of Taste and Enlightenment*. That the man believed he had done right and earned **eternal salvation** <note>original: "ewige Seeligkeit"</note> thereby, he attempts to prove from the twenty-second chapter of the **First Book of Moses** <note>the Book of Genesis, specifically the story of the binding of Isaac</note>. 

Even now, when the malcontents in the **United Netherlands** wish to insult the **Hereditary Stadtholder** <note>the *Erbstadthalter*, the chief executive of the Dutch Republic, likely referring to William V during the political unrest of the 1780s</note>, they make use of biblical prophecies and call him the **Antichrist**. Whether they do so in jest or in earnest, I do not know; I only know that such writings and

It is well known from the history of **ancient astronomy** <note>original: "Sternkunde des Alterthums"</note> and from the great **Platonic Year** <note>A period of approximately 26,000 years in which the stars complete a full cycle due to the wobbling of the Earth’s axis</note> that the ancients, even in the earliest centuries we know of, were aware of the aforementioned movement <note>the precession of the equinoxes</note>. Poets who utilized the **four ages of the world** <note>a traditional Greek/Roman concept of human history declining from a Golden Age to an Iron Age</note>, and who made use of those derived from the **precession of the equinoxes** <note>the slow shift of the constellations relative to the seasons</note>, began with the golden age. They then followed it with the silver, then the bronze, and finally the iron. This was because the Lion appeared yellow or golden; the Bull—namely that white bull into which **Jupiter** <note>the Roman king of the gods, known as Zeus in Greek</note> is said to have once transformed himself, and which indeed appears beautifully white in the sky—appeared white or silver; the old Egyptian water-bucket, or **Canopus** <note>original: "Kanobus", a reference to an Egyptian deity often depicted as a jar, here associated with Aquarius</note>, which is the Aquarius, appeared bronze; and finally, the Scorpion appeared black or iron. 

Others, however, who created their four ages of the world from the four seasons, placed the silver first, then the golden, then the iron, and finally the bronze. They did this because they began counting with Spring, or the white Bull; then they named Summer, or the yellow Lion; then they proceeded to Autumn, which is the black, iron Scorpion; and they ended with Winter, or the bronze water-bucket. 

Therefore, the first rider in the **Apocalypse** <note>the Book of Revelation in the New Testament</note> can very well ride a white horse, the second a red horse, the third a black horse, and the fourth a pale horse. Then I will clearly show that all folk religions basically flow entirely from a common source: from the ancient observations of celestial and natural events. Heaven and nature are those great books in which all nations, where culture began to awaken, have read—and still read—almost entirely the same events from the beginning. ->### Preface. XIII<-

among one nation in these, and among another in those dark shrouds, so that the **profane** <note>original: *Profanen*; here meaning the uninitiated or common people who were not part of the priestly or scholarly classes</note>, who did not belong to their learned tribes, could not find the key to their secret science. I have titled my book *Astrognostic Final Judgment* <note>original: *Astrognostisches Endurtheil*</note> because <term>astrognosy</term> <note>from Greek *astron* (star) and *gnosis* (knowledge); the study of the names and visible positions of the stars</note> is the knowledge of the apparent position and the apparent course of the stars, but does not concern itself, as <term>astronomy</term> does, with mathematical measurements of the true motion, the true size, and the true distance of the stars from one another. Among the ancients, astronomy was almost nothing more than mere astrognosy. This they combined with <term>astrology</term>, or with that deceptive art of prophesying from the constellations. From these two arts—from astrognosy and astrology—they forged their prophecies and their **religious systems**.

I call the movement of the <term>equinoxes</term> <note>original: *Nachtgleichpunkte*; points where the sun crosses the celestial equator, making day and night equal</note> **precession** <note>original: *Präzession*</note> for the reason that I am primarily looking at the constellations that move away from the aforementioned points according to the order of the signs. If one looks at the points themselves, one must say <term>recession</term> or "backward movement" instead of precession, as is clear in itself.

# Preface.

As I have heard and read, you all certainly wish to be good citizens, useful members of human society, and honest people. However, gold-makers <term>Goldmacher: A common term for alchemists who claimed to be able to transmute base metals like lead into gold.</term> are always either useless people or deceivers, whether they are actually able to produce it or not.

If they cannot make any gold, and yet still wish to be regarded as people who understand this art, then it is clear in itself that they must be called deceivers.

If, however, they can make it without great effort and without materials that are already disguised gold <note>original: "verlarvtes Gold." This refers to a common trick where alchemists hid real gold inside chemical mixtures or hollow stirring rods to "prove" their success to gullible patrons.</note>, then they provide the public with something that has no true value, but merely an imaginary one; it is not a true commodity, yet they exchange it for real goods and the true necessities of life, and they thus defraud the public with it. As soon as a great deal of gold can be produced without effort and without high costs, its value drops immediately; it becomes cheap and is no longer a convenient means for the promotion of trade. In itself, gold can be used for nothing except perhaps making something look shiny and yellow. One should simply work and support oneself like other honest people. What would become of the world if everyone made gold and no longer wanted to work? Then they might try to eat gold and clothe themselves in gold. Gold and silver must never fall below the value determined by the needs of the miners, the smelters, and the owners of the mines—the costs they incur while these metals are extracted and refined <note>The author is arguing for a "labor theory of value," suggesting that the worth of money must be tied to the actual human effort and resources required to dig it out of the earth.</note>,

There is no shortage of these metals in the world: consequently, one does the world no favor by producing them. No private individual is permitted to bring gold and silver into public circulation at all: for this business belongs solely to the state, or to its sovereign. But one also need not fear that the Rosicrucians and Brothers of Solomon <note>The "Brothers of Solomon" likely refers to the "Order of the Golden and Rosy Cross," an 18th-century Rosicrucian society that claimed Solomon as a foundational figure.</note>, or whatever else they may be called, actually make these metals. They merely destroy them or calcine <term>verkalchen: An alchemical term for oxidation, where a metal is heated until it turns into a powder or "calx."</term> them, and afterwards reduce them back again <note>This refers to the process of turning a metal into an oxide and then back into a metal, which an amateur might mistake for creating the metal anew.</note>, yet are often ignorant enough to believe they can truly make them in such a way—I can do that trick as well!

However, if they make gold and silver at great expense and at the risk of losing their health—as recently did *James Price* in England (see *London Chronicle* No. 4039 and the *Gotha Scholarly Journals*, No. 26. 1782) <note>James Price (1752–1783) was an English chemist and fellow of the Royal Society who claimed to have discovered a powder that could turn mercury into gold. When pressured to repeat the experiment before witnesses, he committed suicide by drinking laurel water (cyanide).</note>—then, insofar as they make these metals, they are completely useless to the world as well as to themselves, and therefore do not deserve to be listened to at all, especially since they do not make their art publicly known for the expansion of the world's sciences. Were they to make it known, then the assayers <term>Scheidekünstler: Experts in the chemical separation and purification of metals; the precursors to modern analytical chemists.</term> might perhaps go further and invent truly good chemical products through it that would bring real benefit to the world. But they do not do this: consequently, as gold-makers, they are useless and harmful members of human society.

If these gentlemen finally possess a **universal medicine** <term>Universalmedizin: Also known as a panacea, this was a legendary substance alchemists claimed could cure all diseases and indefinitely prolong life.</term>, which I cannot believe of them—since they, like other people, escape neither illness nor death—then they should surely make the preparation of it known to the world as well, so that all people could make use of it, if they were true friends of humanity and not mere **quacks**? To me, indeed, they do not darken the mind: I understand the language that prevails in them well enough, and I know that often only the very simplest chemical processes, which any **apothecary's boy** <note>The author uses this term to emphasize that the "secrets" are actually basic, entry-level chemistry known to any pharmacy apprentice.</note> can perform, lie hidden within them under a shroud of barbaric words and silly **astrological hieroglyphs**. But is every reader shrewd enough to realize this? Does not many a person have their head turned by such writings, and is not many a person drawn away from their business by them? One might as well stay home with such secrets in the future: for today, in the sciences, secrets, miracles, and supernatural revelations no longer hold weight. **Clarity in thinking and writing** is always the first duty of every author, which he must observe if he does not wish to be hissed at.

# Introduction

When all heads of households were still farmers and shepherds, and all farmers and shepherds were still kings, who lived socially with their children and servants among the livestock: at that time, they initially knew no measure of time other than the duration of the apparent daily revolution of the heavens, which we call a **natural day**. Every time the sun set, they placed a stone in a designated spot and afterwards counted the days that had passed by these gathered stones; for they could not properly record the number of their days because they did not yet possess writing.

However, as these stones accumulated immensely over a few generations and could no longer be easily counted, the observers of the heavens soon found themselves compelled to seek a larger measure of time <term>Zeitmaaß</term>. They found it in the periodic changing of the moonlight and now likewise placed a stone in its place every time they observed this change. We call this measure—which actually contains twenty-nine days along with several hours and minutes—a **moon** <note>original: "Mond"; used here to mean a lunar month.</note>; but those earliest inventors of it likely estimated it at only twenty-eight days, despite the fact that long after them it was extended to thirty days by the **Chaldeans** <note>The Chaldeans were an ancient people of Mesopotamia famous for their early advancements in astronomy and mathematics.</note>.

From the changing of the moonlight also arose the **week**, which likewise provided a convenient measure of time. If the moon is new today, then after seven days it turns half of its illuminated side toward the earth and is called the **first quarter**. After twice seven days

After four times seven days, we see him once more not at all, and call it the **new moon**. Nothing, then, was more natural or more sensible than for people to turn this short period of seven days into a measure of time <term>Zeitmaaße</term>, especially since they could use it quite conveniently to designate the elapsed quarters of the moon. Consequently, the Mosaic creation story <note>The account of the world's origin found in the biblical book of Genesis.</note> played no part in the origin of the week, nor can it have any: for creation still continues uninterrupted even now, and will likely never be completed for all eternity. But of course, to realize this, one must be well-versed in modern astronomy as well as in natural history.

Following this, those ancient observers of the heavens also noticed that the sun itself seemed to travel around the sky from west to east—slowly, to be sure, but nonetheless regularly. Since they spent most of their lives under the open sky and could therefore observe the course of the stars at leisure, they gradually became aware that during each such revolution of the sun, an equal number of days, weeks, and moons <note>In this context, "moons" refers to lunar months.</note> always passed. They therefore also made this period of revolution into a measure of time; that is, they invented the **year**, and afterwards likewise marked each one with a stone. In the present day, we have certainly determined its duration precisely; but one must not seek such exactness in remote antiquity. Initially, it was estimated at only three hundred and fifty days, or twelve twenty-nine-day moons along with two leap days; but later, when thirty days were reckoned to a moon, it was given three hundred and sixty days.

# Introduction

Now large cities emerged, and among most peoples of antiquity, those well-known priestly orders arose. These orders took over the administration of all sciences as well as divine worship, passing this knowledge down as a hereditary right to their descendants. They did not easily instruct laypeople <term>Laien: non-experts or those outside the religious order</term> in these matters; instead, they turned their knowledge of nature into sublime secrets, into which they were accustomed to initiating their children with pompous ceremonies. Furthermore, the place where those stone markers <term>Marken: physical tokens, like stones, used to count time</term> of elapsed measures of time <term>Zeitmaaße</term> were kept acquired a kind of sanctity—just as the aforementioned markers themselves were held in exceedingly high esteem due to their great age. For this reason, the priests did not reduce those older markers of days, weeks, and moons into markers of years (as would have been proper to do after the invention of the year). Instead, they left them all lying together because they would otherwise have had to throw some away. And old things, once they are in a holy place, are not thrown away even by us enlightened peoples, however much they often disgrace not only common sense but also chronology <note>The author is likely making a satirical jab at 18th-century religious traditions that clung to outdated or illogical dogmas.</note>.

When later descendants of these first priests came upon the markers—which had been collected partly by their ancestors and partly by the very earliest observers of the heavens—they took them all to be markers of regular solar years. This happened because they did not know that in former times, people had not counted solely by solar years, but also by moons, and even by weeks and individual days. This is the reason why many a nation boasts of such a great age for its religious system and political constitution; it is also why Moses attributes such a great age to the so-called patriarchs <note>The "patriarchs" refer to biblical figures like Methuselah, who were said to live for hundreds of years.</note>. # Introduction

Although more than a millennium may have passed from the beginning of human culture until the invention of the solar year, people at that time still knew no form of writing. Consequently, they had no means by which they could have recorded the quantities of elapsed moons and years in a convenient way to hand them down to posterity. Instead, they found themselves forced to count all things present in large quantities on their fingers. Since they had no more than ten of these, they always counted only up to ten; in this way, decades <term>Dekaten: groups of ten</term> were born. From just as many decades as a person usually has fingers, centuries <term>Centurien: groups of a hundred</term> were formed, and finally, from every ten centuries, millennia <term>Millenen: groups of a thousand</term> arose. Thus, humans came to the aid of their memory—which was not yet accustomed to grasping large numbers without physical images—with their fingers. And so, those periods of ten, one hundred, and one thousand moons and years, which one finds here and there in antiquity, received their existence. This method of calculating and counting, perfectly suited to human nature, spread so far that the ancestors of Romulus, and later the Romans themselves, even made a period of ten moons into their civil year. We still have awkward traces of this today in the Latin names of the last four months of our year. <note>The author refers to the months September, October, November, and December. In Latin, these names mean the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth months respectively, reflecting an ancient ten-month calendar that began in March.</note>

They were now able to achieve this goal in a simpler manner. When they wished to hand down their dates, or reports of remarkable events, and simultaneously indicate their duration, this was done, as is well known, partly through oral tradition and partly through pictorial representation. In the first case, they used their fingers or other groups of ten things as markers. In the second case, they likely drew decades <term>Dekaden: groups of ten</term> as a pair of hands with outstretched fingers, while centuries <term>Centurien: groups of a hundred</term> were perhaps drawn like ten claws or horns, and so on. But indeed, these fingers may often have looked merely like straight lines, while the claws or horns—which in later times were also made into symbols of strength—likely resembled nothing more than thick hooks. For in those days, people were certainly much further behind in the visual arts than in astronomy <term>Sternkunde: the study of the stars</term> and all other sciences, despite the fact that these, too, were still lying asleep in their cradle.

Finally, writing was invented: the only certain means of handing down reports of remarkable events and elapsed measures of time to posterity in a truly intelligible way. People continued to observe the course of the celestial lights, and now they wrote down the results of these observations in an orderly fashion to leave them to their descendants. These descendants later compared their own observations with those of their ancestors and newly discovered various measures of time consisting of great periods, which were used for the calculation of eclipses, the conjunctions <term>Konjunktionen: the meeting of two celestial bodies in the sky</term> of the planets, and other celestial events. These spirits, they believed, partly ordered the regular course of the stars and partly spread winter and summer, autumn and spring, scarcity and abundance, crop failure and fertility, heat and frost, and so on, over the earth according to their own will. They did not stop there: for the inclination toward the extraordinary and the miraculous is innate in all human beings. Rather, they now also believed that the political constitutions of entire nations, as well as the fates of individual people themselves, rested in the hands of these gods, and alternated in an orderly way just like their periodic orbital times. Some of those who forged this system likely knew that it had no firm foundation; otherwise, they could have said everything clearly and would not have had to wrap their prophecies <note>original: "Weissagungen"</note> in confused images or double-tongued speech. The older sky-observers <term>Himmelsbeobachter: early astronomers who recorded planetary movements</term> had, in their orally transmitted accounts, merely used imagery to convey that after a certain number of moons and years—or after so many decades and centuries—these or those stars would complete their labors <note>original: "Arbeiten," referring here to their orbital cycles or revolutions</note>, and begin anew once more. But the true sense of these traditions and images had, by then, largely faded away among the priests. These men imagined nothing but gods within the stars, and nothing but the management of earthly events within their "labors." From these principles it followed, of course, that the gods, by completing their labors, brought entire states to ruin through great plagues, but through the new beginning of those cycles, they drew those states forth from nothingness once again.

they created a vast quantity of these based on the most absurd provocations. If, for example, it did not rain for several moons and a famine followed, they immediately turned the number of these moons or days into a prophetic number <term>Prophetenzahl: a specific numerical value believed to hold mystical or divinatory significance</term> which inherently contained hunger and misery. Thus, every tragic event gave rise to seven different periods, because they counted seven planets and assigned a specific nature to each one. The happiness and pleasure of entire nations do not stand out as much as tribulation and general national distress; therefore, they rarely created periods with a positive meaning. This makes it sufficiently clear why most of these periods are of a horrific nature. In the same way, they created new prophetic numbers whenever it rained too much for several moons, or when the lands where they resided were laid waste by pestilence, war, and locusts. In short, the obscurities and confusions that crept into this science due to the many absurd additions became incredibly vast.

All the so-called mystical numbers in the Apocalypse <note>original: "Apokalypse," referring here to the biblical Book of Revelation</note> and in the writings of the Prophets are of this same kind. The same fate that the original measurements of time of the ancients had to suffer through these astronomical mistreatments by later <term>priests <note>original: "Sacerdoten"</note>: a term used here to describe a formal class of ritual leaders who corrupted earlier natural observations</term> also befell those symbols through which the earliest sky-observers, for lack of writing, strove to transmit their reports of occurring celestial and natural phenomena to posterity — Yet I must explain myself more clearly regarding this sentence, and thus return once again to the highest antiquity, in order to investigate how those strange prophetic images might actually have originated.

Above, we have seen that first the sun, and afterwards the moon, drew the eyes of men before all other celestial bodies. Since the sun, with its bright radiance, darkened every star that stood above the horizon at the same time as it, and consequently did not allow anything else to be observed in the sky in its presence other than its daily course from east to west, or perhaps its rising and falling from south to north and from north toward south; the moon, on the other hand, at least left the stars of the first three magnitudes <note>a measurement of stellar brightness; stars of the "first magnitude" are the brightest in the sky</note> visible every night, especially when it appeared only half-full or crescent-shaped. Thus, nothing was more natural than that the observers of its course and its phase-change would particularly notice those stars where it underwent a <term>heliacal <note>original: "heliakisch"</note>: an astronomical term for when a celestial body disappears into the glare of the sun or emerges from it</term> setting every time—that is, where it hid itself under the sun's rays on the morning horizon. For the ancients always considered this <term>heliacal</term> setting to be the end of the old moon, just as they considered its <term>heliacal</term> rising, or its emergence from the sun's rays on the evening horizon, to be the beginning of the new one. Every time it set <term>heliacally</term>, they would, as mentioned, place a stone in a sacred place chosen for that purpose:

Now, however, the moon does not always set <term>heliacally <note>from the Greek 'heliakos,' meaning 'of the sun.' A heliacal setting occurs when a celestial body—like the moon or a star—disappears into the brightness of the morning or evening twilight because of its proximity to the sun.</note></term> near the exact same constellation: for each time, it moves forward by about a twelfth part of the <term>zodiac <note>original: "Thierkreis," literally 'animal circle'; the belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs.</note></term> toward the east. For this reason, the ancients immediately organized the stars they found in these twelve locations in the sky into twelve distinct groups. For the sake of convenience in thinking and speaking, they imagined each of these under an image that had some relation to the natural events occurring at the end of each lunar month in their land and among their livestock.

Thus, the star group at which the moon set heliacally while the sheep were lambing was designated with a lamb—which, however, was later transformed into a **Ram** <note>the zodiac sign Aries</note>. After four weeks, the moon set heliacally once again, and around this time most cows calved: therefore, the star group where it now disappeared was shaped like a calf, or also like a young **Bull** <note>the zodiac sign Taurus</note>. Again, after approximately four weeks, the goats gave birth: consequently, the constellation where the moon now appeared for the last time in the morning twilight was given the shape of two young goats, which other peoples soon thereafter transformed into the two twin brothers, **Castor** and **Pollux** <note>the zodiac sign Gemini; named after the famous twins of Greek mythology</note>. From these few examples of the works of the earliest **star-gazers** <note>original: "Sternseher"; an early term for astronomers</note>, it follows that the other images of the stars could have arisen, and certainly did arise, from similar circumstances.

Once the star groups and planets, as well as atmospheric phenomena <note>original: "Lufterscheinungen"</note> and various other things occurring in nature, had been rendered into images in the manner described, they were simultaneously used as a convenient means of passing down reports of remarkable natural events to posterity. For example, if one wanted to describe the **conjunction** <note>original: "Zusammenkunft"; literally a "gathering" or "meeting" of planets</note> of several planets, their images were drawn in their proper connection, and to this was added the animal or constellation <note>original: "Gestirn"</note> in which they appeared together within the **zodiac** <note>original: "Thierkreis"</note>. In the same way, its **heliacal setting** <term>heliacal setting: the last time a celestial body is visible in the western sky just after sunset before being lost in the sun's glare</term> was painted like a man whom the sun killed or cast down from heaven. In this manner, all natural events were treated. # Introduction

From the mysteries of *Isis* were formed the mysteries of *Ceres*, which subsequently arrived in *Athens*. The greater mysteries of this kind clearly also had the knowledge of the single God—the creator of all things and the soul of the world—as their primary subject. However, in this context, *Deism* <term>Deism: The belief in a supreme being or creator based on reason rather than revelation.</term> was no longer a natural consequence of the beneficial effects of the sun, but rather a result of the philosophical reasoning of thinking Greeks, who were able to successfully decode the true meaning of the ancient Egyptian symbols representing the effects of nature. Within these mysteries, the triple divine essence of procreation was undoubtedly taught as well; this is proven partly by depictions of male and female reproductive organs, and partly by grains of corn, cakes, pomegranates, ivy, poppies, and other fruits of nature that were carried about in the mysteries of *Bacchus*, *Isis*, and *Ceres*. Regarding *Pythagoras*, who fashioned his mysteries from East Indian, Persian, *Chaldean*, *Egyptian*, *Orphic*, *Eleusinian*, and *Samothracian* sources, it is at least reliably known that he taught the Trinity and Unity of God.

Whoever wished to be initiated into the mysteries of *Mithras* <note>original: "Mithra"; refers to the Roman cult of the god Mithras, which involved complex initiation grades.</note> had to endure eighty difficult trials, as *Nonnus* <note>original: "Nonus"; likely referring to Nonnus of Panopolis, whose commentaries describe the grueling trials of the Mithraic initiates.</note> reports. That is, he had to fast <gloss>fast</gloss> <note>original: "f n"; an abbreviation for "fasten."</note> for many consecutive days, frequently swim across a wide river, run through fire, live in solitude, and so forth. Once the candidates had survived these trials, they were then baptized and marked on their foreheads with secret signs. Honey was smeared upon their tongues; such ceremonies were also observed during the admission of new members in other types of mysteries, as is known from the history of *Pythagoras*, who sought initiation in every place where such societies existed.

# Introduction

At the celebration of the mysteries of **Isis**, it was customary to dramatically represent **Osiris**, who was torn apart by a cruel dragon, **Typhon**, but whose bloody remains were then gathered again by **Isis**. **Osiris** was the sun. The dragon represented the node of the moon's orbit, still called the <term>Dragon’s Head or Dragon’s Tail: Historical astronomical terms for the ascending and descending lunar nodes, the points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path (the ecliptic), which is where eclipses occur.</term> where, as is well known, all solar and lunar eclipses fall. **Isis** signified, as I have already said, the moon. Thus, this entire drama contained nothing more than a report of an eclipse of the sun, which the dragon—or the node of the moon's orbit—as it were, "ate"; but after the completion of the eclipse, the moon, as usual, gathered the remaining sunlight again and became visible anew. In the lesser mysteries of **Ceres**, on the other hand, the fable of the abducted **Proserpine** <note>Proserpine is the Roman name for Persephone, whose descent into the underworld was used by the ancients to explain the winter dormancy of crops.</note> was dramatized; she was anxiously mourned by her mother, **Ceres**, which basically indicated nothing more than a spoiled harvest or scorched grain. Because of this, the fields where it had grown grieved immensely out of compassion for the poor people who now had nothing to eat.

One sees from this that the images and fables of the ancient mysteries as a whole really contained nothing more than well-known celestial and natural events, as **Dionysius of Halicarnassus** and **Plutarch** <note>Dionysius (a historian) and Plutarch (a philosopher) both sought to explain the "hidden" meanings of religious rituals through history and science.</note> explicitly assert. This is also quite natural: for heaven and nature were, from the beginning, the great books in which all nations could read clearly and from which they could abstract consistent concepts. It is therefore not even necessary to claim that all similar ideas of dissimilar and far-distant nations must necessarily have come from a single ancestral people: for the similarity of such concepts exists in the heavens and in nature itself.

# Introduction

The mysteries of *Isis* were transformed into the mysteries of *Ceres*, which later arrived in *Athens*. The greater mysteries of this kind clearly had as their main subject the knowledge of the one *God*, the *Author* of all things, the *Soul of the World*: but here, *Deism* <note>Deism: The belief, based solely on reason, in a God who created the universe but abandoned it, assuming no control over life or nature.</note> was no longer a natural consequence of the beneficial effects of the *sun*, but rather a result of philosophical reasoning by thinking *Greeks*, who were able to successfully unravel the true meaning of the ancient Egyptian symbols of natural forces. In these mysteries, they undoubtedly also taught the triple divine essence of *procreation*: for this is proven partly by the images of the male and female reproductive organs, and partly by the grains of wheat, cakes, pomegranates, ivy, poppies, and other fruits of nature that were carried around in the mysteries of *Bacchus*, *Isis*, and *Ceres*. Regarding *Pythagoras*, who created his mysteries from *East Indian, Persian, Chaldean, Egyptian, Orphic, Eleusinian*, and *Samothracian* sources, it is at least reliably known that he taught the *Trinity* and *Unity of God*.

Anyone wishing to be initiated into the mysteries of *Mithra* <note>Mithra: An ancient Persian god of light and truth whose cult became popular across the Roman Empire.</note> had to endure eighty hard trials, as *Nonus* <note>Likely referring to Nonnus of Panopolis, a Greek poet whose work was often cited in early modern studies of ancient mythology.</note> reports; that is, he had to <unclear>fast</unclear> for many consecutive days, swim through a wide river many times, run through *fire*, live in solitude, and so forth. Once the candidates had survived these trials, they were then baptized and marked on their foreheads with secret signs. Honey was smeared onto their tongues: and such ceremonies were also observed in other types of mysteries during the admission of new members, as is known from the history of *Pythagoras*, who sought admission wherever such mysteries existed.

# Introduction

At the celebration of the mysteries of *Isis*, it was customary to dramatically represent *Osiris*, who was torn apart by a cruel dragon, *Typhon*, whose bloody remains were then collected again by *Isis*. *Osiris* was the sun. The dragon represented the node of the moon’s orbit, the still-so-called <term>dragon’s head or dragon’s tail</term> <note>These are historical astronomical terms for the lunar nodes—the two points where the Moon's orbit intersects the ecliptic (the sun's apparent path). Solar and lunar eclipses can only occur when the moon is near these nodes.</note>, where, as is well known, all solar and lunar eclipses fall. *Isis* signified, as I have already said, the moon. Thus, this entire drama contained nothing more than an account of a solar eclipse, which the dragon, or the node of the moon’s orbit, as it were, devoured; but after its completion, the moon, as usual, collected the remaining sunlight again and became visible anew. In the lesser mysteries of *Ceres*, on the other hand, the fable of the abducted *Proserpine* <note>In Greek mythology, Persephone; she was the daughter of Ceres (Demeter) and was abducted by Pluto (Hades) to the underworld.</note> was dramatized, who was anxiously mourned by her mother, *Ceres*. This signified nothing more than a ruined crop or burnt grain, over which the fields where it had grown grieved immensely out of compassion for the poor people who now had nothing to eat.

One sees from this that the images and fables of the ancient mysteries in their entirety really contained nothing more than well-known celestial and natural events, as <term>Dionysius of Halicarnassus</term> <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric (c. 60 BC–after 7 BC).</note> and *Plutarch* <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer (c. 46 AD–119 AD) whose works often sought to explain myths through natural philosophy.</note> explicitly claim. This is also quite natural: for heaven and nature were, from the beginning, the great books in which all nations could clearly read and from which they could abstract consistent concepts. It is therefore not even necessary to claim that all similar ideas among dissimilar and widely separated nations must necessarily have originated from a single <term>ancestral nation</term> <note>original: "Stammvolke" — a common progenitor or "root people" from whom all culture supposedly spread.</note>: for the similarity of such concepts is found in the heavens and in nature itself.

# Introduction

At the celebration of the mysteries of **Isis**, it was customary to dramatically represent **Osiris**, who was torn apart by a cruel dragon, **Typhon**, whose bloody remains were then gathered again by **Isis**. **Osiris** was the sun. The dragon represented the node of the moon's orbit—still known today as the <term>Dragon’s Head or Dragon’s Tail</term> <note>These are traditional astronomical terms for the ascending and descending lunar nodes; they are the two points where the Moon's orbit intersects the Ecliptic (the Sun's apparent path).</note>—where, as is well known, all solar and lunar eclipses occur. **Isis** signified, as I have already stated, the moon. Thus, this entire drama contained nothing more than a report of a solar eclipse, which the dragon (or the node of the moon's orbit) "devoured," so to speak; but after its completion, the moon, as usual, gathered the remaining sunlight once more and became visible anew. In the "Lesser Mysteries" of **Ceres** <note>Ceres is the Roman name for the Greek goddess Demeter; her "Lesser Mysteries" were held annually at Agrae as a preparation for the "Greater Mysteries" at Eleusis.</note>, on the other hand, they dramatized the fable of the abducted **Proserpina** <note>Also known as Persephone; her abduction to the underworld by Pluto (Hades) caused her mother's grief, resulting in winter.</note>, who was anxiously mourned by her mother, **Ceres**; in essence, this indicated nothing more than a ruined harvest or scorched grain, over which the fields where it had grown grieved immensely out of compassion for the poor people who now had nothing to eat.

One sees from this that the images and fables of the ancient mysteries, taken as a whole, really contained nothing more than well-known celestial and natural occurrences, as **Dionysius of Halicarnassus** and **Plutarch** <note>Dionysius was a 1st-century BC historian; Plutarch was a 1st-century AD philosopher. From this, it again seems clearly evident that their primary intent was to study nature in order to more closely understand its fundamental essence—that is, God, or the <term>universal world-soul</term> <note>Known in Latin as the *Anima Mundi*, this is the idea that a spiritual essence permeates all nature, connecting the divine to the physical world.</note>—as **Clement of Alexandria** <note>A Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who often wrote about the relationship between Greek philosophy and religion.</note> also implies.

Now we wish to return to our text concerning the origin of these fables and images, which we left off above during the discussion of the **Christian Trinity**, and for now acquaint ourselves with just one more example of this.

The most magnificent star after the sun and moon was **Venus**, which, because of its extraordinary clarity and size, very quickly drew the attention of the earliest stargazers. When they wanted to tell posterity that it had once risen high above the horizon in its most beautiful radiance before sunrise, and had thus been the **Morning Star**, they painted the heavens and placed a man within them whose beauty and stature almost equaled the image of the sun, to indicate that it had shone in the sky almost like a small sun. I also need not point out that in ancient times, the seven <term>geniuses</term> <note>original: "Geniuse". In ancient cosmology, these were guardian spirits or divine beings thought to govern the movements of the planets.</note>—by whom the seven <term>planets</term> were carried around the sky according to the customs and teachings of that time—were turned into the seven most noble spirits, or <term>archangels</term>, who stood before the Lord to carry out his commands. This means they constantly flew around the earth and directed not only all natural events but also the <term>fates</term> of mankind.

The green, <term>turquoise-colored</term> man <note>The author is likely referring to the description in Daniel 10:6, often linked to Revelation 1, where a figure's body is described as being like "beryl" (a gemstone that can be green or blue-green).</note> who is being discussed here thus signified the Earth, which back then, just as now, had a green appearance in most regions due to green herbs and trees. His light garment, which surrounded him, indicated the clouds or the <term>atmosphere</term>; and his glowing thighs had to represent the golden mountains upon which the earth was believed to rest in those days. The golden belt represented the hot zone, where the sun’s rays formerly set almost everything into a glow. The back of his face was the temperate zone, or the serene climate of the oldest <term>stargazers</term> <note>original: "Sternseher"</note> who first painted this image; while his snow-white hair signified the highest northern regions, where snow remains throughout summer and winter. The seven stars that he held in his hand were the seven planets, which were always tied to the earth, just as the seven lampstands—which were sometimes also painted as seven burning torches—indicated nothing more than the seven geniuses by whom the planets [were...]

### Second Vision

After the ancient stargazers <note>The author uses "Sternseher" (star-seers), a term that bridges the gap between ancient astrology and early astronomy.</note> had advanced somewhat in the sciences and already knew that the earth was round like a sphere, they believed that it stood in the middle of the cosmic structure <note>Original: *Weltgebäude*, referring to the universe or the "world-system."</note>. They took the heavens to be a spherical crystal vault—a hollow, blue sea of glass—to which the stars were fixed all around, facing the earth. 

Thus, when they wanted to represent the cosmic structure, they painted the Earth in the middle of a tablet in the form of a **green man** who had a rainbow around his head and sat upon a throne <note>Original: *Stuhl* (chair). In the context of Revelation and this astronomical map, it refers to the seat of authority or the central point of the cosmos.</note>. Not far from the throne, they placed the four constellations of the **zodiac** <note>Original: *Thierkreis*, literally "animal circle."</note>: the **Bull**, the **Lion**, the **Scorpion**, and the **Water-Bearer**. These were the most notable constellations of the entire sky at that time because within them lay the points of the **solstices** <note>Original: *Sonnenwenden*</note> and **equinoxes** <note>Original: *Nachtgleichen*</note>, as has been shown in the introduction to this present work. 

Outside the zodiac, the **Chaldeans** and **Persians**—as **Diodorus Siculus** <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE; the author is citing him to provide a historical, secular basis for the imagery in Revelation.</note> reports—counted another twenty-four constellations in the sky. Twelve of these, which according to their legend never set but always stood in the northern sky above the horizon, were at that time the lords and rulers of the day, or of the living. The other twelve, however, which were located in the southern hemisphere of the sky below the horizon and never rose but always remained invisible, had command only over the night and over the dead. But all twenty-four taken together were the judges of all mankind, of the dead and the living, and were likewise placed around the earth. Finally, they also led the sky itself around the entire painting in the form of a blue circular wall. Also we-

# Revelation IV. 1—8

...not to forget the seven **genii** <note>Original: *Geniusse*. In ancient cosmology, "genii" or spirits were often associated with the seven known planets.</note> of the planets, which they placed in the form of seven burning torches around the Earth—that is, around the man who sat upon the throne. But the throne itself meant nothing more than the **rest** <note>The author is highlighting the geocentric view where the Earth remains stationary (at "rest") while the heavens move.</note> of the Earth, which, as is well known, was believed in ancient times to sit entirely still, while letting the whole sky and all the images of the zodiac—which therefore had no rest day or night—wander incessantly around it.

Thus, the images of this supposed second vision were nothing more than the **astrological symbols** of the heavens and the terrestrial globe, and in regard to the future, they also mean—nothing.

The **green man**, who sat on the throne and had a rainbow around his head, was therefore once again the ancient symbol of the Earth. However, here he stood in the middle of the hollow celestial sphere, which consequently gave our author—or at least the older prophets from whom he presumably borrowed the entire **fable** <note>Original: *Mährchen*. The author uses this word to signal his skeptical, rationalist view that the vision is a borrowed myth rather than divine revelation.</note>—reason to place the scene of the appearance now in the sky. For no rainbow is merely green, but rather red, yellow, green, blue, and violet—and almost all these colors are also found in the two aforementioned types of stone when they are quite beautiful, especially the well-known **ribbon jasper**. ### Revelation IV. 1—8

The **twenty-four elders**, who sat in a wide circle around the seat of the Earth and were clothed in white garments, represented the aforementioned twenty-four constellations. According to the delusions of the **stargazers of Babylon** <note>The author attributes the imagery of Revelation to Babylonian astrology, which influenced Jewish thought during and after the Exile.</note>, these were the supreme judges of mankind; because of their love of justice, they wore not only golden crowns but also white garments. Black or multicolored clothing would certainly not have suited these figures, as they were supposed to consist entirely of stars and thus necessarily had to be enveloped in white light.

The **sea of glass** or **crystal**, which the author otherwise claims to have seen before the throne, was nothing more than the **sky**, which the ancient stargazers universally represented as a blue firmament <term>firmament: from the German "Veste," referring to the ancient belief in a solid, hammered-out dome over the Earth</term>—a crystal vault.

Finally, regarding the **lightning** that came from the throne, accompanied by peals of thunder as well as other loud noises: it becomes clear once again that these were merely intended to be understood as the thunderstorms and gale-force winds that often occur. It also shows that the author was instructed about these images either orally or in writing; for through mere sight, he could perceive neither the thunder nor the voices.

This latter conclusion will also hold true for many subsequent visions; therefore, from now on, I will always take it as a given and not constantly speak of it.

# Second Vision

Once, the stargazers <note>original: "Sternseher." Historically, these were observers of the heavens who combined what we now call astronomy and astrology.</note> observed a very large Northern Light <note>original: "Nordlicht." Also known as the Aurora Borealis; this passage suggests that ancient descriptions of divine glory may have been inspired by this atmospheric phenomenon.</note>, which traveled from the North in the form of broad fiery rays and reached all the way to the Zodiac <note>original: "Thierkreis," literally the "animal circle."</note>. These fiery rays were red and left large white spaces empty between them, which hardly obscured the light of the stars standing behind them at all. This Northern Light was followed by rainy weather, and this in turn by a rainbow with sunshine. Therefore, in order to leave a record for their descendants of this atmospheric phenomenon—which was perhaps rare to them—they first marked the four regions of the world on a tablet and then painted in a large fiery cloud that came up from the North. In the middle of this cloud, they left a bright white space to indicate the white spots in which the stars appeared. However, so that one would also know that this fire-cloud reached up to the Zodiac, they painted the most prominent animals of the same—the animals of the solstices and equinoxes: the Bull, the Lion, the Scorpion, and the Water-bearer—onto the aforementioned white space. But in the South, East, and West of the tablet, they painted a wide-spread sea, which represented the part of the sky that the Northern Light left clear. Finally, to indicate the rain that followed this phenomenon, they placed the Sun in the highest place of heaven in the form of a man on a blue chair <note>This "man on a blue chair" mirrors the description of God on a sapphire throne in Ezekiel 1 and Revelation 4.</note>, and let rays go out from him that descended into the clouds and formed all the colors of the rainbow.

Two of these formed the four colures <term>Koluren|Two principal meridians of the celestial sphere that intersect at the poles; one passes through the equinoxes and the other through the solstices.</term>, one the Equator, and one the solar path <note>The ecliptic, or the apparent path the Sun follows across the sky over a year.</note>, upon which latter the twelve constellations of the Zodiac,

Initially, it was depicted simply as a man with ram’s horns; however, the astrologers, who now enriched their hieroglyphic treasury with it and incorporated it into their mysteries, designated its prophetic meaning by means of a triple allegory as follows:

The ram itself was retained but presented as if killed, partly to note its annual <term>heliacal setting</term> <note>original: "heliakische Untergang"; the time when a star or constellation disappears into the sun's light at sunset</note>—for which they painted a wolf that had to strangle it—and partly to indicate through this strangulation the universal death that nature would suffer when all seven planets would gather again in this constellation. To indicate that the planets would indeed meet there in the future, this dead sheep was given seven eyes, which simultaneously signified the seven great spirits of the planets, the seven supreme gods, and the seven archangels. Finally, seven horns were placed on its head to show that all constellations ended after the seven orbital periods of the seven planets, and thus lasted for seven periods every time.

Each of these periods was later turned into a millennium <note>original: "Jahrtausende"</note>, partly out of ignorance of astronomy and partly because one happened to have ten fingers <note>The author suggests that the decimal system led humans to arbitrarily group years into units of ten or one thousand</note>. Thus it came to pass that the entire age of the world was given seven millennia, and each of these was ruled by one of the planets.

->Revelation VI. 1 — 14<-

The ancient Egyptians used this image to show the fleeting nature of the nine months of their field work. Instead of a calendar, they placed a symbol in a public place for each moon <note>meaning each lunar month</note>, which indicated the specific tasks that fell within that month. To this, they likely also added the winged horse each time, seeking thereby to encourage the people to be industrious.

But the Greeks transformed these symbols of the nine working months into nine industrious maidens, the **nine Muses**; the aforementioned symbol of fleetingness, however, they turned into the **Muse-horse** <note>original: "Musenpferd"; referring to Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek mythology associated with poetic inspiration</note>. Finally, the symbols of the remaining three months—during which the Egyptians could not work because of the flooded Nile, but instead enjoyed themselves upon the hills—were transformed into three young dancing maidens, the **three Graces**.

Thus, the four horses in the Apocalypse are likely nothing more than symbols of four different periods of time. But why specifically a **chestnut**, a **white horse**, a **black horse**, and a **pale horse**? We wish to investigate the matter further.

It was shown extensively in the introduction that the division of the **Zodiac** <term>Zodiac: the "circle of animals" or belt of constellations through which the sun, moon, and planets appear to move</term> into twelve **constellations** was one of the first tasks of the ancient stargazers. It was also shown that the number of these images did not arise by chance, nor was it made larger or smaller, because the moon sets **heliacally** <term>heliacal setting: when a star or planet disappears into the sun's bright light at evening</term> twelve times a year near twelve different groups of stars. The ancient Egyptians used this image to show the fleetness of the nine months spent in field labor. In place of a calendar, they would place a symbol for each moon <note>referring to a lunar month</note> in a public area, which indicated the specific tasks to be done during that month. To this, they likely also added the winged horse <note>this refers to the concept of time flying; the author links this to the origins of Pegasus</note>, seeking to encourage the people toward diligence in their work.

But the Greeks transformed these symbols of the nine working months into nine industrious young women, the nine Muses. The aforementioned symbol of fleetness, however, was turned into the "Muses’ Horse" <note>the winged horse Pegasus, who in myth created the spring of the Muses with his hoof</note>, and finally, the symbols for the remaining three months—during which the Egyptians could not work because the Nile had overflowed, and instead passed the time enjoying themselves on higher ground—were turned into three young dancing women: the three Graces.

->### Revelation VI. 1—14<-

For at that time, one by no means dared to count them consecutively up to twenty-four, and thus to mix the kings of the underworld with the princes of the upper world <note>the author refers to the ancient belief that constellations below the horizon ruled the "underworld" while those above ruled the "upper world"</note>; yet this would have had to happen if the hours were to continue to be ruled by them. Therefore, people preferred to have these [hours] ruled by the planets, specifically in such a way that the first was given to Saturn, the second to Jupiter, the third to Mars, the fourth to the Sun, the fifth to Mercury, the sixth to Venus, the seventh to the Moon, the eighth again to Saturn, the ninth again to Jupiter, and so on, continuing through all hours and all days in the same sequence until the first hour fell once again to Saturn, and thus the week was completed. It should only be noted here that the planets followed one another in the exact same order in which the Chaldeans <note>ancient Mesopotamian astronomers</note> and East Indians at that time arranged them according to their distance from above down toward the Earth: namely <term>♄ ♃ ♂ ☉ ☿ ♀ ☽: the astrological symbols for Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Mercury, Venus, and the Moon</term>, that is, **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, **Mars**, **Sun**, **Mercury**, **Venus**, and **Moon**.

### Second Continuation of the Second Vision
->catchword: hour<-

Thus, if one allows the planets to rule the hours one after another in the order mentioned: the same planet that falls on the first hour will also fall on the eighth, fifteenth, and twenty-second hours every time, and this planet always gives the day its name, as may be clarified by the attached diagram.

<image-desc>
An astrological diagram representing the twenty-four hours of the day and their planetary rulers across the week. At the top is a horizontal row of twenty-four planetary symbols in the Chaldaean order <note>The "Chaldaean order" arranges the planets by their perceived orbital speed/distance from Earth in ancient geocentric astronomy: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon.</note>: Saturn (♄), Jupiter (♃), Mars (♂), Sun (☉), Venus (♀), Mercury (☿), and Moon (☽), repeated to fill the line. 
Below this is a grid with rows corresponding to the days of the week, labeled on the left with symbols for the Sun (☉), Moon (☽), Mars (♂), Mercury (☿), Venus (♀), and Jupiter (♃). Each row contains dots aligned with the columns, with the day's ruler repeated at specific intervals (representing the 1st, 8th, 15th, and 22nd hours). At the end of each row on the right is the symbol of the planet ruling the 24th hour of that day. 
A final row of planetary symbols runs along the bottom of the diagram. The layout demonstrates how the 24-hour cycle shifts the ruler of the first hour to the next day's namesake.
</image-desc>

Here, the horizontal lines contain the twenty-four hours, while the vertical columns from the top down contain the seven days.

Saturn, being the uppermost <note>In the geocentric model, Saturn was considered the "highest" or outermost planet.</note>, began and ruled the first, eighth, fifteenth, and twenty-second hours of the first day; this day was therefore called **Saturday** <note>original: "Samstag"</note>, because the day was always given the name of the planet to which the rule of its first hour fell. Since the twenty-fourth hour of the first day was the second hour after the twenty-second, and Mars was the second planet after Saturn <note>in the descending Chaldaean order: Saturn (22), Jupiter (23), Mars (24)</note>: the rule of this last hour fell to Mars. Consequently, the first hour of the second day fell to the planet that followed immediately after Mars, which was the Sun; the Sun thus gave the name to the second day, that is, **Sunday**. This planet now likewise ruled the eighth, fifteenth, and twenty-second hours of this day: consequently, the rule of the twenty-fourth fell to Venus, and thus the rule of the first hour of the third day fell to the Moon, which was therefore called **Monday**.

### Revelation 6:1–14

The [twenty-fourth] hour of that same day fell to **Jupiter**, who was followed by **Mars**; he therefore ruled the first hour of the fourth day, and thus bestowed upon it the name of **Mars-day**. <note>The author is explaining the origin of the names of the days of the week; Tuesday is *dies Martis* in Latin or *mardi* in French.</note> The second planet after **Mars** was **Mercury**, followed by **Venus**: the former ruled the last hour of the fourth day, while the latter ruled the first of the fifth, which consequently received the name of **Venus-day**. <note>Friday, or *dies Veneris* / *vendredi*.</note> The last hour of the fifth day fell, according to the order, to **Saturn**, and consequently the first of the sixth to **Jupiter**, who therefore gave this day the name of **Jove’s day**. <note>Thursday, or *dies Iovis* / *jeudi*. "Jove" is an alternative name for the god and planet Jupiter.</note> On this day, the **Sun** ruled in the last hour, which was followed immediately by **Mercury**: he thus received the governance of the seventh day, and therefore gave it the name of **Mercury-day**. <note>Wednesday, or *dies Mercurii* / *mercredi*.</note> The last hour of this day fell to the **Moon**: consequently, the first hour of the eighth day fell again to **Saturn**, who thus began the week anew.

According to this arrangement, the names of the days followed one another in this fashion: **Saturn’s day**, **Sun-day**, **Moon-day**, **Mars-day**, **Venus-day**, **Jove’s day**, and **Mercury-day**.

From the aforementioned order of the planets, one can see that the oldest astronomers in **East India** and **Babylon** estimated the distance of **Mercury** from the Earth to be greater than the distance of **Venus**: but the **Egyptians** reversed the matter and placed **Venus** further away from us than **Mercury**. Both parties were sometimes right and sometimes wrong in this regard, and could therefore easily waver back and forth between this or that opinion: for **Venus** is, as is well known, often truly much closer to us than **Mercury**, just as the latter is often much closer to us than **Venus**. One would think that this small astronomical dispute would have changed nothing in the world—

...flowed from the sun as it were upon the earth, since one made the sun the supreme God: and now it would probably have been sinful if one had further robbed him of this honor, and had not wanted to make his day the first of the week. In short, Sunday now became the first, and thus Saturn-day the last, day of the week, and all seven followed one another according to the latter schema in the following manner: **Sunday**, **Monday**, **Mars-day**, **Mercury-day**, **Jove-day**, **Venus-day**, **Saturn-day**.

The ancient Germans, our ancestors, revered **Mars** under the name of **Dien** <note>Dien refers to the Germanic god Tiw or Tyr, from whom we get "Tuesday".</note>, **Mercury** under the name of **Wodan**, **Jupiter** under the name of the great **Thor**, and finally **Venus** under the name of **Freia**: consequently our **Sunday** is the day of the Sun; **Monday**, the day of the **Moon**; **Tuesday**, the day of **Dien** or of **Mars**; **Wednesday** <note>original: "Mittewoch" (Mid-week)</note>, which only in some Lower Saxon provinces is still called **Woens-** or **Wodan's Day**, is the day of **Wodan**, or of **Mercury**; **Thursday** or **Thor's Day**, the day of the great **Thor**, or of **Jupiter**; **Friday**, the day of **Freia** or of **Venus**, and finally **Saturday** <note>original: "Sonnabend" (Sun-eve)</note>, which however only the Swabians and Franks quite correctly call **Saturn's-day** or **Samstag**, the day of **Saturn**. Yet this latter remark concerning the German names of the seven days of the week was only made in passing, and is not intended to help contribute anything to the achievement of our purpose.

But this is well to be considered: that the ancient **priests** <note>original: "Sacerdoten"</note>, who alone were in possession of the sciences of that time, now also dedicated the known seven metals to the seven planets, in that the Sun was **Gold**, the Moon was **Silver**, **Mars** was **Iron**, **Venus** was **Copper** or **Ore**, **Jupiter** was **Tin**,

### Third Continuation of the Second Vision

As for the sealing, the author seems to have taken this from **Nehemiah** <note>Referring to the biblical book of Nehemiah, specifically chapters 9 and 10, where the leaders of Israel set their seal to a renewed covenant with God</note>.

What else could his Jewish pride find in these twelve constellations besides the twelve sons of **Jacob**, since **Joseph’s** dream <note>A reference to Genesis 37:9, where Joseph dreams of the sun, moon, and eleven stars—representing his family—bowing down to him</note> taught this so tangibly? What else could the individual stars of these constellations be to him but **Jews**?

The fact that exactly twelve thousand stars were assigned to each constellation came about because they wished to suggest that each contained an uncountably large number of stars. They played with the number twelve, just as such games with other numbers were very fashionable among **astrologers** at all times, especially with the numbers **three** and **seven**. The former because of the three persons of procreation <note>A likely reference to the ancient concept of the triad: father, mother, and child as a fundamental unit of existence</note>, and the latter because of the seven **planets**.

But the great multitudes who had gathered from all kinds of nations and stood before the Lamb to serve him were the **geniuses** <term>geniuses<gloss>original: "Geniusse"</gloss></term> <note>In ancient and Enlightenment-era thought, a 'genius' (from the Latin genius) referred to a tutelary spirit or divine essence governing a person, place, or, in this case, a celestial body</note> of the remaining stars of heaven. These could not, of course, bear the twelve names of the twelve tribes of Israel, and consequently had to be **Gentiles** <note>original: "Heiden" (Heathens/Pagans)</note>. They were clothed in white garments because the stars have always shone white, and were thus dressed in white.

One might object that the author could not well have used these **geniuses** of the stars—those located outside the **zodiac** <note>original: "Thierkreisse"</note>—for a second time, as they were already contained within the twenty-four **elders**, who after all signified nothing more than the twice-twelve **geniuses** of the constellations placed outside the **zodiac** by the **ancients**. That exactly seven such angels blew their trumpets arose from the fact that the ancient astronomers <note>original: "Sterndeuter," meaning those who interpreted the stars; the author suggests the writer of Revelation was influenced by pagan science</note>, from whom our author had learned his art of prophecy, assigned seven lesser servant spirits to the seven supreme gods—the planets. These spirits then blew a short fanfare in honor of their masters, each individually, in the exact order in which their masters were once arranged in Egypt in ancient times, according to their distance from the Earth.

Just as many calendar makers even now assign to each planet dominion over certain plants, animals, countries, rivers, and so forth, for the sake of maintaining superstition, so too did the ancient astrologers dedicate to each planet a certain class of creatures. These, as is well known, consisted in antiquity of three different principles: an airy, a watery, and an earthy principle—or of **spirit**, **soul**, and **body**. The spiritual or airy principle came from the **Father** of natural products, the **sun**; the watery or lunar <note>original: "selenitische," derived from the Greek moon goddess Selene</note> principle from the **Mother**, the **moon**; and finally the earthy or terrestrial principle from nutrients. Thus, the first two had a heavenly origin—that is, they were spiritual emanations of the two great lights of the world, or their guiding spirits <term>guiding spirits<gloss>Geniuse</gloss></term>—and could therefore not be destroyed, but had to last eternally. But the third part <note>A reference to the "third" of the earth/sea/trees destroyed in the previous biblical verses</note> was certainly subject to decay or corruption: and for this reason, it could indeed always

### First Continuation of the Third Vision

...still lie there, as if bound, as I will soon show.

Initially, the Milky Way of heaven was compared only to a great stream: but later this comparison was also extended to the **zodiac** <term>zodiac<gloss>The "circle of animals" or the belt of the heavens through which the sun, moon, and planets appear to move.</gloss></term>, because it was likewise seen in the shape of a wide band, or stream, flowing unstoppably from East to West across the heavens. In this way, in the minds of the **Chaldeans** <note>The Chaldeans were ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia, widely regarded by historical scholars as the founders of astrology and astronomy.</note>, who knew no greater river than the Euphrates, there arose the idea of the great river where the aforementioned four gods were supposedly bound.

A twelfth part of the day passed whenever each of these **animals** <note>The constellations of the zodiac.</note> rose daily from beginning to end—that is, as it rose above the horizon. A whole day passed as each one circled the entire sky once from East to West. A **month** <note>original: "Mond" (moon). In this context, it refers to the lunar month.</note> passed as the moon completed its course once around the whole sky from West to East, and consequently passed through each of them. Finally, an entire year passed before the sun completed its annual path through each of them. Since a twelfth part of the day was also called an hour: they certainly had something to command over an hour, a day, a month, and a year. 

Therefore, at the end of the last **world age** <note>original: "Weltalter," referring to a great cycle of time in cosmic history.</note>, according to our author's concepts, they had to be released to be ready for an hour, a day, a month, and a year to kill the earthly third of mankind, because he [the author of Revelation] had once and for all decided to have those people killed who were not sealed Jews. However, so that these might suffer a truly shameful death, he had the many thousands of thousands of **horsemen** <note>original: "Reisigen," referring to the cavalry or mounted troops mentioned in Revelation 9:16.</note> of these four released angels armored with fiery sulfurous breastplates...

# Revelation 10:8 — 13.
G 5

...[prophe]sy, because it was given to the Gentiles, who would trample the holy city for forty-two months. <note>This refers to Revelation 11:2, where the outer court of the temple is abandoned to the non-believers for a period of three and a half years.</note>

What is to be thought of the "voices from heaven," which were then in fashion among the Jews, is well known. Although it cannot well be denied that a divine power dwells within man, which at times speaks very loudly and presents him partly with distant objects and partly with future events that concern him directly—in short, that many a person sometimes has premonitions—the superstitious Jews nevertheless tended to exaggerate the matter far too much. They took all the "speaking ideas" that suddenly awoke in their over-excited imaginations for voices from heaven. Among Christians, these are not infrequently regarded as the workings of the Holy Spirit, especially among those whom an awakened conscience torments because of evil deeds. The Greeks called them warning voices of <term>daemons: in the ancient Greek sense, these were guiding spirits or divine inner voices, such as the "daimonion" described by Socrates, not the modern concept of evil demons</term>.

Our author seems to have learned the "eating of books" from <term>Ezekiel: an Old Testament prophet whose book contains many of the strange symbols—such as flying chariots and scrolls—that influenced the author of Revelation</term>, who likewise ate a parchment scroll written with lamentations, sighing, and woe; it tasted sweet as honey in his mouth, but caused him no stomach cramps, presumably because it was not too large and consequently not difficult to digest. The little book, however, which our author swallowed, and in which the fates of the world or of mankind were determined astrologically—perhaps as in the <term>Key of Solomon: original: "Claviculis Salomonis," a famous medieval grimoire or book of magic and planetary signs attributed to King Solomon</term>—undoubtedly consisted of at least several rolled-up calfskins, which would certainly cause "stomach-pinchers" for any of us if we were to eat some. But joking aside! This whole business of eating books was merely an exaggerated Oriental metaphor, which meant nothing more than that one had read a book with great desire...
