The author of the book on *The Purpose of Jesus and his Disciples* <note>A reference to Hermann Samuel Reimarus (1694–1768), whose radical Enlightenment critique of Christianity was published posthumously by G.E. Lessing. Reimarus argued that Jesus was a political revolutionary and that the disciples stole his body to maintain their status.</note> asserts the latter. However, I cannot agree with him. Had the disciples done this, they would undoubtedly have been the most exquisite villains, the most base liars, and the most cunning deceivers. They could hardly have fallen into such malice, much less found the means for such a deception, as they had not attended high schools <note>In this context, formal universities or academies where rhetoric and logic were taught.</note> and thus had not methodically learned sophistry or the art of chicane. They were merely fanatics <note>The German term *Fanatiker* here implies "enthusiasts" or people driven by religious fervor and imagination rather than calculated malice.</note>, and they themselves believed that the miraculous events had indeed occurred—events which, if they did not entirely invent them, they at least monstrously enlarged in order to dress up their writings nicely, according to the fashion of all historians of that time. This is precisely how fanatics differ from other people: their own fictions seem to them to be established truths.

But stealing a corpse and afterwards saying he had risen does not well fit such crookedly thinking and crookedly acting people. Furthermore, **John** is actually far less superstitious and possesses, in fact, far more philosophical sense, as well as more frankness, than the other Evangelists. Nevertheless, he also reports to us that Jesus not only left the tomb but also appeared to his disciples in **Judea** as well as in **Galilee**. One must, however, accord more credit to this Evangelist regarding the resurrection story in general than to the others; for although he likewise exaggerated his reports far too much and [adapted] all the events that happened to Jesus to his Gnostic system <note>The author suggests that the Gospel of John was written to align with "Gnostic" philosophical ideas, a common perspective in 18th and 19th-century biblical criticism which viewed John as more metaphysical than the other Gospels.</note>...

### Jesus and his Disciples. 347 ###

...sought to adapt himself too closely <note>The author suggests that the Gospel writer may have tailored his account to fit certain expectations or earlier traditions.</note>, he still went with Peter, at the request of Mary Magdalene, into the tomb itself. Not only did he not find Jesus there, but he says he later saw him walking and eating in both Bethany and Galilee. However, he knows absolutely nothing of the Ascension <note>original: "Himmelfarth"</note>. From this, it follows that Damm <note>Christian Tobias Damm (1699–1778), a prominent German Enlightenment theologian and philologist who sought naturalistic explanations for biblical miracles.</note> is likely closest to the truth when he says: Jesus was not entirely dead, but only in a state of deep unconsciousness <note>original: "stark ohnmächtig"</note> when he was buried.

But were his wounds not then lethal? The wounds on his hands and feet were not; this is something everyone will easily admit. As for the wound in the side <note>original: "Lendenstich" - literally "loin-stab," referring to the spear-thrust in the side described in the Gospel of John 19:34.</note>: it is well known that many people are occasionally stabbed and are nevertheless healed again. Baltschmidt <note>Likely Johann Wilhelm Baltschmidt, an 18th-century physician or medical author who wrote on the physiology of wounds.</note> even claims to have healed transversal wounds <note>original: "Quervellswunden" - likely referring to "through-and-through" wounds that pass entirely through a body part.</note>. It simply depends on whether the heart, the stomach, or a major artery is damaged. In such a case, recovery would certainly not easily occur. But if every stab and every shot necessarily struck the most noble organs of life, there would perhaps be many thousands fewer people in the world today than there actually are. It must also be considered that the soldier <note>original: "Kriegsknecht"</note> did not stab Jesus in order to kill him completely. No, he stabbed him merely to see if he still felt anything, and whether he was therefore truly dead. Therefore, he surely did not stab him very deeply? It is also probable that he did not stab him in the abdomen or under the ribs, as is commonly imagined, but rather in the thick flesh of the flank <note>original: "Lendenfleisch"</note>, because a stab there hurts far more intensely, and thus causes a much stronger sensation, than a stab in the belly or under the ribs, despite being less [dangerous] <note>The page ends with the catchword "gefähr-", indicating the next page begins with "gefährlich" (dangerous).</note>

### Jesus and His Disciples. 348 ###

...is more dangerous than this one. One must further consider that **Jesus** indisputably had a delicate body and a very sensitive nervous system, which could not long endure the tension of the arms, or rather the resulting stagnation of the blood; and so it is clear that he very soon fell into a faint, which was so profound that he did not even feel the spear-thrust. But this very thrust provided relief <note>original: "Luft" — literally "air," but used here to mean an outlet or release for the pressure of the blood.</note> to the stagnating blood. **Joseph of Arimathea** immediately took him down from the cross, and **Nicodemus** wrapped him in aromatic spices, which gently stimulated his nervous system and gradually set his blood back in motion. Can one therefore still doubt that **Jesus** could have come to himself again in the tomb? After all, was **Pilate** not already reluctant to torture him severely or kill him entirely? 

But he had to condemn him to the cross because the **Jews** said: **"You are no friend of Caesar if you let this man go, who seeks to make himself a king!"** <note>A reference to John 19:12, where the crowd pressures Pilate by questioning his loyalty to the Roman Emperor.</note> Had he perhaps even secretly signaled <note>original: "unter den Fuß gegeben" — an idiomatic expression meaning to give a secret hint or private instruction.</note> **Jesus** in the judgment hall that he should merely feign death soon, so that he could have him taken down from the cross immediately afterward? One might well suspect such a thing when reading how reluctantly he allowed him to be crucified, how he sought to excuse him in every possible way, and how deliberately he did not have his legs broken, although this happened to all others who were crucified. 

That the soldiers should have omitted this latter act on **Jesus** merely because he appeared to have already died is not at all probable. # Jesus and His Disciples. 349 #

...how willingly Pilate gave the body of Jesus to Joseph of Arimathea as soon as he heard that he had died. This was a favor that surely no other crucified person could have expected! The aromatic poultices afterward stimulated his nerves again; these set his stagnant blood back into motion, and he was then, of course, able to walk out of the tomb again.

## Jesus and his Disciples. ##

...honor, almost as if quite deliberately seeking it. This can only be the effect of fanaticism <note>original: "Fanatismus." In the 18th century, this term was a heavy critique, referring to religious extremism that abandoned reason.</note>. Greedy people love Mammon <note>A biblical term used to personify wealth and material greed.</note>, when it comes down to it, more than the truth; for the sake of pleasing God, they will allow themselves neither to be stoned to death, nor crucified, nor beheaded. Rational-thinking people know that it is all the same to God whether one honors him under this or that name, or whether one worships him under this or that form, as long as one is a human being—that is, as long as one promotes the good in the world with all one's might. This good, however, is never to be sought in specific creedal opinions, nor in suffering and dying, but rather in well-being, in life, in the right use of reason as well as the necessities of this life, in the freedom to think, in brotherly love, and in pure pleasure. Fanatics, however, find their greatest pleasure and their greatest merit precisely in specific religious opinions, which they therefore seek to impart to other people even at the risk of their lives. They value this pleasure far higher than life itself.

The story of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit <note>Referring to the event of Pentecost described in the Book of Acts, where the disciples were said to be filled with the Spirit and speak in tongues.</note> is held by our author of the Fragments <note>Hermann Samuel Reimarus.</note> to be entirely fabricated. While today this translates as "excitement," in this context it refers to a state of ecstatic, possibly irrational, religious fervor.</note>. People who harbor the same sort of fanatical <note>original: "schwärmerische." This term was used by Enlightenment thinkers to describe a visionary or delirious religious zeal they considered dangerous.</note> opinions regarding religious matters, and who gather in great numbers with one accord for divine service, impart to one another the power of their overstrained imagination and reinforce the mutual urge of their souls. Set aglow by this urge, as if by flames of fire, they are carried away into holy enthusiasm and incited to all sorts of strange gestures, songs, deeds, and sensations.

<page-num>399</page-num>
->Europe's Newer Enlightenment.<-

The completely raw state of the uneducated nomad, who knows no other excellence but physical strength, and the flourishing of agriculture, livestock breeding, manufacturing, trade, the arts, and the sciences, are indisputably the two opposing boundaries of the culture of the human race. The flourishing of agriculture, livestock breeding, manufacturing, trade, and the arts primarily strengthens and beautifies the body, as these things provide sensory pleasure. The flourishing of the sciences, on the other hand, preeminently elevates and sharpens the soul. Therefore, the culture of man can properly be divided into two distinct levels: a lower and a higher. 

On the lower level stand all new inventions that noticeably promote sensory pleasure, or even just convenience; on the higher level, however, stand only the sciences that promote the growth of the spirit <note>The German word used is "Geist," which in this period refers simultaneously to the mind, the intellect, and the spirit.</note>. In the future, for the sake of variety, we will often simply call the lower level **Culture**, and the higher level **Enlightenment**. Culture can exist among many nations without Enlightenment needing to show them her beautiful face. But where the latter is to show herself publicly, the former must necessarily have already prepared the necessary dwellings and made all sorts of good arrangements, because Enlightenment is the daughter of Culture, and consequently receives her life, as well as all her needs, from her mother.

Now the first question is: Has the world, or at least Europe, gained in Culture and Enlightenment since the introduction of Christianity?

### Europe’s Newer Enlightenment.
<meta>Note: There is a discrepancy in the original pagination; the previous page was marked 399, while this is 360. The thematic continuity, however, remains intact.</meta>

Scholars who diligently study the Greeks and Romans, but in doing so too greatly neglect not only the modern sciences and arts themselves but also their history, almost universally claim that the Greeks and Romans, long before the emergence of Christianity, were just as clever, just as learned, just as wise, and just as enlightened as we are. Indeed, it is even claimed that we are nothing more than parrots, merely babbling everything after them but never thinking for ourselves; and that we must, in fact, babble after them if we wish to produce anything good, because they have already exhausted the source of the Good and the Beautiful. This is often further proven using that saying of the famous Solomon, who already in his lifetime claimed that *nothing new happens under the sun* <note>original: "daß unter der Sonne weiter nichts neues geſchähe." A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:9.</note>. In such a manner, we would not even be as clever or as enlightened as the Greeks and Romans who lived before Jesus, if their pretentious admirers were right and if we really only imitated them without thinking for ourselves. Nevertheless, these very same admirers of antiquity often also claim that Christianity has contributed a great deal to the culture of the human race in Europe. But how could it have promoted this culture if we were not more cultured and more enlightened than the ancient Greeks and Romans?

However, these scholars—these partisan admirers of antiquity—plainly act with the greatest injustice against themselves, or at least against their fellow colleagues who are well-versed in the modern sciences. This is precisely because they do not understand the matter any better, and because they neglect the newer sciences. Even if it were granted that our philosophers could not reach the level of a Pythagoras, a Socrates, a Plato, a Zeno, an Epicurus, and so on, much less

# Europe’s Newer Enlightenment. 367

The admirers of antiquity <note>Those who believe the civilizations of ancient Greece and Rome represent the highest point of human achievement.</note> may rebel against this proposition as much as they wish.

Moreover, this culture and enlightenment has grown immensely, not only in terms of its height <note>Referring to the depth and sophistication of knowledge.</note> but also in regard to its length and breadth. In former times, almost only the noble and the wealthy could enjoy the happiness that springs from culture, because the few manuscripts through which the sciences were propagated were held at a very high price, and because the enjoyment of oral instruction always required a great expense, which the poor and lowly could seldom afford. Today, however, all people who are not mere beggars can read well-written books and enlighten their understanding without significant cost. Shop assistants now sit in their shops or warehouses and read books while waiting for customers. Baker-girls, sitting at the bread-stall and offering their wares, have their pamphlets in their hands—even if only to keep up with the fashion. Grocers and shopkeepers, male and female alike, wait in their booths for the sale of their goods while reading. Market-laborers, maids, and servants often spend their idle hours reading popular books to learn something from them with which they can make themselves pleasing to their masters and mistresses. To be sure, they largely read only comedies and novels; however, writers of comedies and novels are nonetheless also sometimes good didactic poets and satirists, who therefore effect some enlightenment of the understanding—or at least some culture of a lower degree—among this subordinate class of people, which in former times was quite impossible.

Consequently, Europe is currently not only much richer in culture and enlightenment than it was before Christianity...

[...attained,] but it is at the same time much richer in the number of cultivated and enlightened people now than it was back then.

But now the question arises: **Did Christianity perhaps cause this culture and enlightenment?**

I am completely convinced *after the fact* <note>original: "a posteriori"; a Latin term referring to knowledge derived from observation or experience</note> that Christianity has truly established more good in the world, and spread more culture—at least over the lower or subordinate classes of people—than paganism did. This is despite the fact that I would not want to prove *beforehand* <note>original: "a priori"; a Latin term referring to knowledge derived from theoretical deduction rather than experience</note> that the same culture could not have made just as much progress if people had retained their paganism; for the Greeks and Romans in former times showed sufficiently that a great deal of culture is indeed possible alongside paganism. 

But I also know for certain that there is a God who governs the world. He has not only arranged all the events that occur within it from eternity, but He also continually carries them out Himself through His own power for the benefit of the whole—whether they seem to us great or small, noble or lowly, miraculous or understandable, and so on. God certainly "works all in all," <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 12:6, "it is the same God who works all in all."</note> and through His own power He directly executes the immense orbit of the planetary worlds around their suns, as well as the life of the smallest worm. 

I also know for certain that this very God is an all-good Providence, who always wills the greatest possible well-being of the whole, and without whom not a single hair on my head can or may be bent. This all-wise Providence has now actually spread Christianity across a fairly large portion of the inhabitants of our little "world-body" <note>the Earth</note>. Consequently, by virtue of this spread, the greatest well-being of the whole—which was ever possible according to the arrangement of the "world-machine" <note>a common Enlightenment-era metaphor comparing the universe to a complex, divinely-constructed clockwork mechanism</note>—is certainly [attained...]

->### Europe’s Newer Enlightenment.<-

[...attained.] Furthermore, Providence, which can only desire the greatest possible good for the whole, would undoubtedly not have allowed Christianity to come into the world otherwise. Consequently, good has been established in the world through it. In the same way, I also believe that Providence will provide for the circulation of the book I am writing, if it can promote the welfare of mankind, taken as a whole. But should it prove an obstacle to the welfare of the whole, then Providence will also take the best counter-measures, because it desires nothing but the greatest possible good of the whole, and consequently can allow nothing to happen except what promotes this welfare. To be sure, however, the greatest possible good of the whole is sometimes necessarily connected with the harm or pain of one or another individual part; for often a link must allow itself to be forged <note>The author uses a metaphor of ironworking; just as a link is struck and heated to join a chain, individuals may suffer for the sake of the greater social structure.</note> so that the whole chain may become useful. Furthermore, it was either truly good or, according to the course of things, necessary that the Eastern Magi, the Jewish prophets, the apostles, the Church Fathers, the contemporary theologians <note>original: "Gottesgelehrten"</note>, the philologists, and others, have not been able to seat themselves outside the house of old astrological traditions and images, in which they had allowed themselves to become entangled by the stargazers and greedy priests <note>original: "Sacerdoten"; a Latin-derived term for priests, often used here with a slightly critical tone regarding their control over tradition.</note>. Had the opposite been possible or good, Providence would surely have allowed the opposite to occur. But I also know that it will be good if Providence allows it to happen now; if it now helps scholars out of this astrological house, and in the future transforms the days, which hitherto had to be spent on the explanation of the prophets and evangelists, at least into hours, thereby permitting the exegetes <note>original: "Exegeten"; scholars who interpret and explain biblical or legal texts</note>, who work twelve hours a day, to devote eleven-twelfths of their labor to useful business.

->### Europe’s Newer Enlightenment.<-

Christianity has certainly established good in the world, for Providence would not have allowed it to come to pass otherwise. However, it by no means follows from this that it is the main cause of the Enlightenment <note>The author refers to the *Aufklärung*, the 18th-century intellectual movement emphasizing reason and individualism over tradition.</note>; for the Enlightenment may owe its existence to entirely different things that have no connection to Christianity at all. What Christianity actually contributed to culture and Enlightenment cannot be known, because one does not know to what degree culture and Enlightenment would currently stand if Providence had not allowed Christianity to arise. 

This much, however, seems certain: that it was initially a very effective means of spreading culture in terms of *length* and *breadth*, but by no means in terms of *height*. This is because it merely disseminated the morality of the noble Greeks among the common folk <note>The author suggests that Christianity served as a popular delivery system for Classical Greek ethics, making high philosophy accessible to the masses.</note> with benefit, thereby drawing them away from a too-coarse sensuality. In other respects, however, it offered no teachings that could promote Enlightenment in terms of its "height," for its other doctrines were for the most part **contrary to reason**, as we have already sufficiently shown. 

On account of these irrational doctrines, it eventually became—once it gained strength—the most significant obstacle to higher culture or the Enlightenment of the intellect <term>Verstand: the faculty of understanding or intellect, often contrasted with 'Vernunft' (universal reason) in German philosophy.</term>. It placed reason in fetters from childhood onward, which indeed only very strong spirits were capable of breaking. Those who owed their status, their power, their prestige, and their wealth to these fetters <note>The author likely refers to the clergy and the ruling classes who benefited from religious orthodoxy.</note> nestled into them with pleasure and could not even begin to conceive that they were fetters at all. The laity, on the other hand, to whom these chains occasionally caused great pain, did not dare to shake them off because they held their lives dear—and so, poor reason had to bow deeply before Christianity.

Had these new causes not become effective, and had these aforementioned new sources not broken forth, then the old causes—namely the growth of the population and the increase in life’s necessities—would have likewise produced a culture that fluctuated, now sinking, now rising. In total, it might have risen more than it fell, yet its rise could nonetheless have been only very slight, as the entirety of antiquity teaches us up until the breaking forth of these mentioned new sources.

The first great benefit that flowed to the world from the **art of book printing**, and from the enlightenment that arose through it, was the **Reformation** of **Christianity**. Although one cannot actually attribute to the Reformation itself any great direct merit regarding the freer use of **reason** <note>The author suggests that early reformers were not necessarily proponents of modern intellectual "reason," but their actions created the conditions for it.</note>: it nevertheless showed Europe’s sovereigns how they could withdraw from the supremacy of the **Roman See** <note>The jurisdiction and authority of the Pope in Rome.</note>, and how those riches—which had to be paid to the **Holy Father** for the forgiveness of sins <note>A reference to "indulgences," the practice of paying the Church to reduce punishment for sins, a central grievance of Martin Luther.</note> or other such things—should be put to a better use within their own countries. And indeed, they did just that; thus the Reformation, though not directly, certainly indirectly brought about no small amount of enlightenment. This is especially evident in the **freedom of thought** that shines forth in Protestant countries, which is protected not by the Church, but solely by enlightened rulers.

We must now cast a glance back at **Italy** and **France**, because the beginning of modern culture and enlightenment spread from these countries across **Britain**, **Germany**, and other European realms. Italy and France had never entirely lost Roman culture—the former because of its location, which is very convenient for trade, and the latter because of its mild climate <note>During the Enlightenment, many theorists believed that "mild" or temperate climates were naturally more conducive to the development of advanced civilization and "lively" temperaments.</note>. But in both, activity and industry would not have risen so noticeably from the tenth to the sixteenth centuries if people had not been encouraged by **German silver**. The Germans’ desire for foreign goods, and our German **silver ingots** <note>Original: "Silberkuchen." Literally "silver cakes," referring to the refined blocks of silver produced by German mines, which were a primary driver of European trade.</note>, revitalized the already lively spirits of the Italians and French anew; they, in turn, became increasingly refined while enlightening other **nations**.

### Europe’s Newer Enlightenment.

Portugal also vied for its share of progress, seeking a more convenient route around the **Cape of Good Hope** to the **East Indies**, so that it might conduct a truly grand trade with all of Europe. This active spirit of commerce finally also inspired **Columbus** of **Genoa**, and led him in the name of the King of **Portugal** <note>The author is historically mistaken here; Christopher Columbus famously sailed under the patronage of King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain, after his proposals were rejected by the Portuguese crown.</note> — not to the East Indies — but into a world which he, as it were, created entirely anew for Europe. This part of the earth, which was like a new creation for the world, has now enriched all of Europe with an extraordinary amount of knowledge regarding entirely new things through the efforts of **French** and **English** merchants. It has opened a great many new paths for acquisition and, consequently, has immensely promoted the **Enlightenment** of the human understanding. By as much as **America** has, as it were, enlarged the physical world, the high and low culture of the Europeans has risen just as much through its discovery. What a pity that the resource-rich surface of our globe is not ten times larger still! We would indisputably be ten times more enlightened, or would at least become so over time! We must therefore take our refuge in the heavens, since the earth is proving too small for us!

### Europe’s Newer Enlightenment.

Also, the damage caused by wars can no longer affect the inhabitants of Europe and other parts of the Old World as severely as before. To the victorious Romans, the Old World was once too narrow. The martial spheres of influence of the powerful were very often concentrated within their own empires, or at least within narrow circles. The most beautiful and cultivated states often raged within their own entrails <note>A metaphor for civil war or internal conflict within Europe.</note> and destroyed themselves, because they did not know that there were still beautiful, rich lands in the world which they could have taken possession of, and because they had not yet found the path leading there. Currently, wars noticeably spare the lands of the Old World their saddest effects, as they mostly spread across the sea and over a **New World**, where there is room enough for them. When people disagree and fight in a narrow room, tables and benches, doors and windows often go to pieces. But if they go out into the wide field, everything in the house remains in its order.

### Europe’s Newer Enlightenment.

**Mines** and the **greed of merchants** for wealth were therefore the true physical causes of the newer culture and enlightenment, but by no means **Christianity**—The **Reformation**, too, was not a cause of higher culture, but rather an effect of it.

### Europe’s more recent Enlightenment.

Freedom of trade <note>original: *Handlungsfreiheit*. In this period, this term encompasses both the liberty to engage in commerce and the broader freedom of individual action.</note> and the increased circulation of money set human powers in motion; they are essentially the souls of the **industriousness** <note>original: *Industrie*. In the 18th century, this referred to the quality of being hardworking and diligent rather than large-scale manufacturing.</note> of nations, the wealth of states, and the growth of **reason**. On the contrary, the restriction of trade and the overly filled, dead treasuries of the Great <note>The "Great" refers to the nobility and sovereign rulers who hoarded wealth rather than allowing it to circulate in the economy.</note> are the death of all human activity.

Man is diligent and enterprising so that he may enjoy the fruits of his labor according to his own pleasure. If one dictates to him what he should eat or drink, or what he should wear, his desire to work vanishes; he conducts his business soully and no longer strives for anything new. However, one can make foreign goods expensive for him without harm, provided they are not among the most essential necessities. 

For more on this, one should read the excellent *Essay on a History of the Culture of the Human Race* <note>The author likely refers to Johann Christoph Adelung's *Versuch einer Geschichte der Cultur des menschlichen Geschlechts* (1782), which attempted to chart the stages of human civilization.</note>, where one can find more detailed information on all these matters—even though the author, like many others, seems to attribute too great an influence on the growth of culture to the **Crusades**.

## Thoughts on the Destiny of Man through God.

That a God exists, nature teaches us in things small and great very emphatically—We must therefore briefly consider nature before we can form a correct, albeit weak, concept of the greatness and goodness and glory of its Creator <note>original: *Urheber* (Originator or Author), a common Enlightenment term for God as the primary cause of the universe.</note>—We wish to begin with the **Creation**.

If we could put a million of our **Earth-globes** together and make a new sphere out of them: this sphere would almost equal our **Sun** in size. **Saturn** is a thousand times, and **Jupiter** over a thousand and a half times larger than our **Earth-globe**. **Saturn** has five, and **Jupiter** four **moons**, <note>These numbers reflect the astronomical knowledge of the time; Saturn’s five moons (Tethys, Dione, Rhea, Titan, Iapetus) were known by the late 17th century, and Jupiter’s four Galilean moons had been known since 1610.</note> each of which is many times larger than the **moon** that orbits our **Earth-globe**. **Mars** is likewise almost as large as the **wandering star** <note>original: *Wandelstern*. An archaic term for a planet, used to distinguish them from the "fixed stars."</note> that we inhabit, as is **Venus**; only **Mercury** is seventeen times smaller. If one wished, however, to melt together all these **world-bodies**, which are all similar to our Earth and most likely inhabited by **humans** <note>The "plurality of worlds"—the belief that other planets were inhabited—was a widely accepted scientific and philosophical theory during the Enlightenment.</note>, along with their moons, and cast a single sphere from them: it would still be approximately six hundred times smaller than the **solar-body**. Therefore, all the **planets** of our **world-system** <note>The solar system.</note> taken together with their **satellites** <note>original: *Trabanten*. A term for moons or celestial attendants that follow a larger body.</note> are to be considered as almost nothing compared to the **Sun**: for out of six hundred, one can lose one without feeling a noticeable loss in the total sum. If one could tower thirty **Earth-spheres** upon one another, one would reach as far as the **lunar orbit**: but in the **Sun**, one would have to tower a hundred **Earth-spheres** upon one another to get from one edge

# Thoughts on Destiny

...astronomers measure the worlds and their distances from one another. Now our sun is approximately twenty-two thousand such half-Earth-diameters <note>original: *halbe Erdmesser*; this refers to the Earth's radius, which the author uses as a fundamental unit of cosmic measurement.</note> distant from us. **Saturn** stands ten times further from it, and thus swings in a distance of approximately two hundred and twenty thousand half-diameters of the Earth, or nearly two hundred million geographical miles around the sun. This is unquestionably a great distance in our eyes: but in consideration of the distance of the nearest sun-stars <note>original: *Sonnensterne*; the author uses this term to emphasize that "fixed stars" are actually distant suns similar to our own.</note> it is nevertheless to be regarded as nothing at all. The nearest sun-star is at least eighty thousand times further than the globe of the Earth is from our sun. Thus, if one multiplies 800,000 by 22,000 or 80,000 by 220,000: then nearly eighteen thousand million half-diameters of the Earth result, and that is how far every two sun-stars stand from one another. Some will indeed be somewhat more or less distant from each other: but taken as a whole, one can suitably let this distance apply for all, as one must not count trifles here anyway.

People whose sight carries sharply into the distance overlook six, yes sometimes even seven such heavenly steps <note>original: *Himmelsstufen*; a conceptual framework used to describe layers of stellar distance based on their apparent brightness.</note>, each of which, as stated, is nearly eighteen thousand million half-diameters of the Earth high. Namely, it is customary to divide all suns, or **fixed stars**, into six different classes according to their apparent size, by counting stars of the first size <note>This refers to the "magnitude" system of brightness still used by astronomers today, where lower numbers indicate brighter objects.</note> in the first class, stars of the second size in the second class, stars of the third size in the third class, and so on. Now, the stars of the second size stand as far above the stars of the first size as the stars of the first size stand above us, or above our sun. In the same way, the third size stands,

At the same time, one must not imagine that these smallest stars, which even the best telescopes barely reveal to us, are the last or the most distant: for one perceives through these same telescopes, far beyond the aforementioned smallest stars, new milky-white patches, which are unfailingly also Milky Ways, consisting of infinitely many suns, which one certainly cannot see individually even through the best telescopes because of their unthinkable distance. If we could grind lenses for telescopes that magnified a thousand times more clearly than the best Dollond instruments <note>John Dollond (1706–1761) was a famous English optician known for perfecting the achromatic lens, which revolutionized 18th-century astronomy by removing color distortions.</note>, we would indeed see a thousand times further into the heavens with them, and thus behold a thousand times more celestial bodies than we currently see through the mentioned telescopes: but an end to the celestial bodies and Milky Ways we would still not find, because space undoubtedly extends infinitely far, and is also provided with suns and other celestial bodies infinitely far.

# Thoughts on the Destination

All these suns likely also pull their own planets and comets into orbit around them. These cannot be seen, however, because they do not shine with their own light like suns do; instead, they merely shimmer with borrowed light in their proximity, much like the planets of our own solar system <term>world system; original: *Weltsystem*</term> that receive their light from our sun. For if they did not illuminate other worlds <term>earth-globes; original: *Erdkugeln*</term> with their light, hatch creatures upon them with their warmth, and breathe life into otherwise dead worlds with their beneficial power, one would not see at all what purpose they were created for. After all, they are of no use to our Earth—nor to our entire solar system—and yet they occupy a space infinitely larger than it. Still, it is quite possible that many of these suns also cast burning or self-luminous planets around themselves, which might therefore be visible through very powerful telescopes.

Imagine that a candle burns here in this room, representing our sun. Around this light, let several tiny specks of dust <note>original: *Stäubchen*; the author uses the image of dust dancing in a sunbeam to represent the planets in our solar system.</note>—which we shall compare to planets and comets—whirl in various circles. Suppose, moreover, that the outermost dust mote orbits the light at a distance of one foot; let the others whirl around it at smaller and smaller intervals. If we reckon sixteen thousand feet to a mile <note>The author is likely using a regional German mile, which varied significantly in length before metrication.</note>, then five miles from here, one must place six other such lights—with their own whirling dust motes—in a circle around this central one. These must be placed in such a way that every two lights also stand five miles apart from each other, resulting in all of them being at an equal distance from one another and from the central light. Furthermore, at a distance of five miles, let us place other such lights with their whirling dust motes above and below this central light—specifically, as many as are needed until there are twelve of them in all directions...

# Thoughts on the Destination of Man

...continue, and consequently, they infinitely exceed not only our senses but also our understanding in regard to their multitude, as well as in consideration of the magnitude of the celestial space they occupy. How greatly then must our globe—which is to be considered as nothing compared to a single such sun—lose itself in comparison with infinitely many such suns and world-systems?

Since these suns are nowhere attached, but float freely in the infinite space of the heavens with their swirling planets, the question arises: What holds them? Why do they not fall? This, it is said, is the attractive force, or universal gravity <term>original: *allgemeine Schwere*; the Newtonian concept of gravitation which was a central topic of 18th-century natural philosophy</term>, which maintains them in their places and protects them from falling! Here stands one sun, and further off stands another. Both attract one another and would collide, were they not pulled back by two others standing further out on both sides, which likewise exert an attractive force upon these. But these outer ones would then be attracted by the first two and would have to fall toward them, were they not again held back by others standing even further out, and so on. What I say here of two sides also applies to all other sides, because the sun-stars <note>original: *Sonnensterne*; refers to the stars, which the author recognizes as suns similar to our own.</note> stand around one another in every direction. Thus, in truth, none can be the last. If some were the last, they would be attracted inward solely by the second-to-last and would have to fall toward them, because further out there would be nothing possessing an attractive force to hold them back. Now the next ones inward would be the last: therefore, these would also have to fall inward, and thus, bit by bit, they would all have to [gather] into a clump toward a common center—

One only knows this much: that its effect decreases in the same proportion as the square of the distance between the bodies attracting each other increases. <note>This refers to Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, established in 1687, which states that the force of gravity between two objects weakens rapidly as they move apart.</note> There have indeed been scholars who believed that the celestial space was filled with a certain extremely fine, fluid, and extraordinarily elastic matter—with <term>ether; a hypothesized substance once thought to fill all space to allow the transmission of light and gravity</term>—which not only held the suns apart and against one another through its tension, in order to maintain them in their proper positions, but also pressed the stone that we throw into the air back down to the ground. Yet, what have they gained through this hypothesis, assumed without any basis? Nothing.

One now asks: But what does the essence of the tension or the elastic force of the ether consist of? Must one perhaps assume an even finer ether to allow the first to be tensioned? From whence would this second one receive its tension? Thus one would have to assume infinitely many such fluid matters, and in the end, one would be right back where one was at the beginning—namely, that one does not know what the essence of the attractive force, or universal gravity <term>original: *allgemeine Schwere*</term>, consists of; just as one is not at all capable of researching the essence of forces in general. 

One perceives effects; these certainly always arise from causes, and these very causes are called forces. One knows only their effects, but not the forces themselves. One measures their effects, but the forces themselves can never actually be measured, despite it being common in linguistic usage to say that one has measured "force." Thus, the cause that maintains the suns and worlds in their proper positions, and [it]...

The <term>fallacy<note>original: *Fallazie*, from the Latin *fallacia*, meaning a deceptive argument or logical error.</note></term> lies in the word: **Transient**, or **Transience**. Nothing, as far as one knows from experience, is annihilated, but everything is only destroyed: for God, or ever-active Nature, makes use of the death of one for the life of another, the wreckage and ruins of one for the construction and growth of another. Metals and precious stones, as stable as they may be, can indeed be transformed into <term>lime<note>The original term *Kalch* (modern *Kalk*) refers to a "calx," the crumbly powder or oxide left over after a metal or mineral has been burnt or "calcined" in early chemical experiments.</note></term> or otherwise destroyed: but they, likewise, are never annihilated. Thus, only the **form** of matter and bodies is transient; the **matter** itself, however, is not so at all—at least, this is what is taught by all observations made thus far regarding the origin and the decline of all products of nature and art. 

If one now reasons from the small to the large, from earthly bodies to celestial ones—as those do who wish to prove the annihilation of earthly things—then it follows only that worlds may be destroyed and transformed into others, but cannot be annihilated. Consequently, one cannot prove from experience that the matter of the worlds once did not exist. One can, rather, draw the very probable conclusion from those same experiences that the worlds have existed from **eternity** and have merely suffered many kinds of <term>modifications<note>original: *Modifikazionen*. In 18th-century philosophy, this refers to changes in the "mode" or state of a substance, while the underlying substance remains the same.</note></term>. This conclusion follows from rational observations of nature; and it also follows from the concepts we form of the **divine attributes**.

We have not yet proved that a **God** exists; however, we wish to assume it has been done, as I hope all my readers will, in any case, be convinced of His existence from other philosophical reflections.

That the Sun is actual fire and burns at least upon its surface—as well as the fact that sunspots are not pits, but most likely dense solar clouds which from time to time plunge back onto the solar surface from its atmosphere to provide new nourishment for the fire—is found sufficiently proven in the first volume of the *Cosmological Conversations* <note>original: *Kosmologischen Unterhaltungen*; this refers to a popular 18th-century work of "physico-theology" which sought to explain the universe through both science and divine purpose.</note>, which one may read for further detail. The heat of the Sun does not reach as far as the globe of the Earth, but merely its light. ...smallest particles of a mass of matter, which contains a great deal of combustible material in its composition, are set into such great internal motion by some force that a dissolution or complete separation of them arises: then that phenomenon which we call fire always appears in such a mass of matter. Furthermore, if the combustible material of a burning mass of matter is not very firmly bound to other elements: then its atoms separate very quickly by virtue of their intended internal motion and form fire, which is called **flame**. But if the atoms of all elements of a mixed matter are very firmly united with one another: then their separation proceeds slowly, even though they are often very strongly internally moved or heated, and they form fire which is called **glow** or **glowing**. Materials that contain no combustible material at all in their composition can therefore neither burst into flames nor into a glow, but can merely be warmed and heated. We know, however, of few materials besides water that cannot either burst into flames or into a glow, only that some always burn more than others, depending on whether they contain much or little combustible material, and depending on whether the combustible material is more or less firmly bound to them.

Combustible material <term>Brennbares<note>The author uses the term "Brennbares" (literally "that which is combustible"), which in the 18th century was often associated with "phlogiston," a hypothetical substance believed to be the essence of fire contained within materials.</note></term> is indisputably the primary element of all suns, and consequently also of ours. Water, air, and earth are, to be sure, likely also mixed with combustible material on them, but in a far smaller proportion than on Earth and on the other planets; at the very least, combustible material has the upper hand on the surface of the Sun just as much as, and indeed far more than, water has the upper hand on the surface of the globe of the Earth.

## of Man through God.

Fire furthermore also possesses many properties of electricity: for it is not only excited by rubbing and striking, just like electricity, but it also not infrequently expresses the effects of lightning when it truly comes to its full strength, as is sufficiently proven partly by those phenomena called the "Wolf" <note>In 18th-century metallurgy, a "Wolf" (or *Bär*) referred to a sudden, unintended solidification or violent reaction in a furnace, often resulting in sparks or bursts of pressure.</note>, and partly by the terrible effects of molten copper into which a little water falls. Moreover, it is also known that large fire-ovens <note>Specifically, industrial furnaces or smelting ovens.</note> often thrust sparks and burning brands very high into the air and hurl them about. In short, fire is probably nothing more than **positive electricity**, which, however, always acts constantly and freely.

From this, it is now easy to infer how very positively electrical the Sun must therefore be, and with what inconceivable force it must have once ejected its surplus matter to form planets from it, which, taken all together, amount to no more than a six-hundredth part of the entire solar mass, as we have already heard above. The entire Sun became a volcano, on whose surface craters upon craters formed, which incessantly spewed fire. It is easy to imagine that during the stated formation of our planetary system, a very great period of time must have passed. One can aptly assume that this formation and arrangement lasted just as long as the formation of the sun—that is, approximately one hundred and eighty million years. <note>The author proposes a vast chronological scale for the universe's creation, far exceeding the traditional biblical chronology common in his era.</note> For although the outermost planet <note>original: *der oberste Planet*; literally "the uppermost," referring to the planet furthest from the sun.</note> stands only about seventeen times further from the sun than the Earth, and thus has only traveled a path from the sun to its orbit that is perhaps twenty-four thousand times smaller than that which the outermost **atoms of chaos** <note>original: *Chaosatomen*; the raw matter existing before the ordering of the universe.</note> had to cover before they could reach the sun: nevertheless, the planets had to whirl away from the sun on **spiral paths**, whereas, on the contrary, the atoms of chaos had previously fallen toward the sun in a straight line. If one could stretch out the spiral paths on which the planets distanced themselves from the sun into straight lines, these would certainly reach more than twenty-four thousand times further than the radius of our entire planetary system; and it is clear that just as much time was required for its arrangement as for the formation of the sun—namely if, as can be probably demonstrated from ***inertia*** <term>Latin: the property of matter by which it continues in its existing state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line, unless that state is changed by an external force.</term> and from the **laws of motion**, the planets, taken as a whole, flew away from the sun with the same velocity with which the atoms of chaos previously flew toward it.

**Solar clouds** and **Earthly clouds** share a great similarity. They differ only with regard to the **matter** from which they consist. The former consist for the most part only of <term>combustible matter<gloss>original: *das Brennbare*; likely referring to the contemporary "phlogiston" theory, where fire was considered a material substance contained within flammable objects.</gloss></term>, while the latter consist mostly of **aqueous vapors**. These then fall back again, provide the solar fire with new nourishment, burn or evaporate anew, contract once more into clouds, and in such a manner likewise observe a constant cycle. # [The Destination] of Man through God.

Less dense than Jupiter is Saturn, and less dense than Saturn is Coelus <note>A Latin name for the Greek deity Uranus, god of the sky. In the late 18th century, the naming of this new planet was still a matter of debate.</note>. Thus, the farther the planets stand from the Sun, the lower their densities. Allow me here to depart a little from the main subject of our consideration.

Coelus or Uranus is currently the uppermost <note>meaning the most distant or "highest" in the celestial spheres</note> planet of our planetary system. It was only discovered a few years ago by Herschel <note>Sir William Herschel discovered the planet in 1781</note> through the telescope, and does not yet have a properly established name. I call it, along with Bode <note>Johann Elert Bode, a German astronomer who famously proposed the name "Uranus"</note>, Coelus or Uranus, because according to the mythology of the Greeks, he was the father of Saturn. Saturn fathered Jupiter, and Jupiter fathered the remaining planetary gods. In this way, the grandfathers and fathers of these gods follow one another in their anciently accepted order, if one gives the uppermost one the name mentioned above. Some, however, would prefer to call it Cybele <note>A Phrygian mother goddess</note>, specifically for the reason that the planetary gods do not have enough women among them in Venus and Luna <note>the Moon</note>. Although this reason does not seem very convincing to me—otherwise one could not very well say "the planet Venus" <note>original: *der Planet*, which is masculine in German</note>, but rather "the planetess" <note>original: *die Planetin*, a feminine construction</note>—I have nothing at all against it if, in the future, one prefers to say Cybele instead of Coelus. Now I wish to return to the matter at hand.

It is probable that all planets emerged from the Sun one after another in the same order in which they now follow one another from the top down. # Thoughts on the Destination [of Man]

...[substances] the uppermost <note>meaning the most distant</note> planets arose; from the densest and coarsest, however, the lowest <note>the inner planets closest to the Sun</note> were formed. The looser these masses were, the sooner they were thrown into the heavens by the electrical shocks of the Sun. They also flew that much further away from it the looser they were: for the looser a body is, the less weight it possesses. Light particles are thus always thrown much further and more easily into the heights by electricity than heavy ones, as everyone knows who is familiar with the phenomena of electricity. One must not imagine that the distance of the planets from the Sun is too great for this; for in consideration of the distance of the solar stars <note>other stars in the galaxy</note>, even the distance of Coelus <note>Uranus</note> from the Sun is to be regarded as nothing, and in proportion to the monstrous electrical machine of the Sun, all planets are not actually further from it than the tips of lightning rods are from the clouds.

When the planets emigrated from the Sun, they continued to burn for a long time, and thus they themselves represented small suns, which certainly did not shine as brightly as their mother, the great Sun, because in proportion to their size they did not contain as much combustible material in their mixture as the Sun itself, and therefore could probably not burn over their entire surfaces, but could only spew fire from their entrails in most places. In a word, the planets were all then sown with raging volcanoes upon their surfaces. They were also very electrical at that time, and spewed monstrous masses of slag <note>volcanic debris or cinder</note> from their bellies very high toward the heavens. These great, glowing mountains of slag sometimes united in the heights and became negatively electrical, whereupon they plunged back down together onto their planets, and now [received] a far more violent electrical shock from them...

But by virtue of the attractive force or universal gravity, the air and water atoms nevertheless drew together more densely around the solar body from all sides the closer they lay to it: for the effect of gravity is greater in the vicinity of every celestial body than at a distance; consequently, it also compresses its atmosphere more densely in the vicinity than at a distance. # Thoughts on the Destination

->of Man through God.<-

...oms, which the air presses together, and which is the sum of the weight of all their individual <term>atoms</term><note>In the 18th century, "atoms" referred to the "corpuscular" theory of matter—the idea that all substances are made of tiny, indivisible physical particles, though not yet understood in the modern subatomic sense.</note> taken together. Thus, during its formation, the Sun was already surrounded by a large atmosphere, which was very dense near it and still is, but becomes increasingly thinner further away from it; initially, it contained all the water atoms that are now distributed among the planets.

The densities and sizes of the atmospheres are proportional to the densities and sizes of their celestial bodies. When the fragments or the constituent parts of the planets still belonged to the solar mass, the Sun had approximately one six-hundredth part more mass than it does now. Consequently, its atmosphere back then was also one six-hundredth part denser and larger than it is currently. But when the planets journeyed forth from it, each took with it as many air and water atoms from the denser solar atmosphere as it could carry according to the proportion of its mass—that is, according to the proportion of its density and size. Thus, the atmospheres of the planets arose from the atmosphere of the Sun, just as the planets themselves arose from the body of the Sun.

Since the planets afterwards remained like small suns for a long time—or at least burned in most places on their surfaces—and in part also gave birth to "children," that is, they cast out small planets or <term>satellites</term><note>original: "Trabanten." Literally "guards" or "henchmen," this was the standard term for moons or secondary bodies orbiting a primary planet.</note> from their interiors, they in turn gave up as much of their atmosphere to these as was necessary in proportion to the lost mass—that is, as much as these children themselves could take with them according to their density and size.

# Thoughts on the Destination

Now, our Moon has approximately eighty times less mass than our Earth; therefore, it also has eighty times less atmosphere than the latter, and its atmosphere close to its surface is nearly eighty times thinner than the atmosphere we breathe. When our atmosphere is quite pure and clear, it consists near the Earth of only five-sixths pure air, while the remaining one-sixth is always water, which floats within it invisibly in the form of vapor. If it is cloudy and rainy, the amount of water mixed into it is even greater. At a constant temperature, the amount of water that can be kept dissolved in the atmosphere is proportional to the square of its density; consequently, at the same temperature, the Moon’s atmosphere must contain six thousand four hundred times less water than an equal volume of our Earth’s atmosphere. Therefore, the Moon has very little air and extraordinarily little water. For this reason, it cannot rain, snow, storm, hail, or have lightning and thunder there. Consequently, no vegetation can grow on it and no living creatures can live there—at least none such as ours, for they would have to be able to eat <term>lava and slag</term><note>The author uses the term "Schlacken" (slag), which in 18th-century geology referred to volcanic scoria or the stony, cindery debris left by subterranean fires.</note> if any were to be found there.

On our Earth, the surfaces of rocks and mountains are dissolved by the weather, transformed into fertile soil, and prepared for the growth of nutritious herbs for humans and livestock. Cloudbursts and storms then tear the loose <term>topsoil</term><note>The original "Dammerde" refers to the dark, fertile layer of soil composed of decayed organic matter, often called humus.</note> down from the mountains and rocks and carry it to the lower regions, which are, as it were, filled up and gradually raised by it. The author's mention of lava and slag suggests a volcanic view.</note>—which are exposed from time to time by violent downpours and storms, gradually weather anew and are washed away again. On

# Thoughts on Destiny

<note>The right margin of the original manuscript is cropped, resulting in missing letters at the end of most lines. These have been reconstructed based on context.</note>

...clumped together, but rather was ejected all at once from the burning globe of the Earth.

Much like our Moon, the moons of Saturn and Jupiter likely appear similar, since they all possess little mass and consequently can have little air and few fluid materials similar to our water. But let us now cast a glance at the primary planets themselves.

Jupiter has a circumference forty times larger than our Earth-globe. Nevertheless, it rotates once on its axis within nine hours, whereas our Earth-globe requires twenty-four hours to complete one rotation. Therefore, Jupiter rotates over a hundred times <note>The author’s calculation of "100 times faster" refers to the linear velocity at the equator. Because Jupiter is much larger than Earth but rotates much faster, a point on its equator travels far more distance in less time.</note> faster than the Earth. Because of this rotation, our Earth-globe is even now gradually becoming thicker between the <term>tropics</term><note>original: "Wendekreisen," referring to the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.</note>, while it sinks by an equal amount near the poles. By virtue of the <term>centrifugal force</term><note>original: "Dreheschwung," literally "rotational swing" or momentum.</note>—which is greatest between the tropics and smallest near the poles—the seawater rises from both poles toward the equator, where the sea must then swell between the tropics and gradually flood flat lands there, because not as much flows back as streams there from both sides. Since Jupiter now rotates a hundred times faster than the Earth, the centrifugal force near its equator must be a hundred times greater than that of our Earth at its equator. Consequently, Jupiter must bulge far more at its equator than our Earth-globe; and astronomical measurements indeed confirm that this planet is extraordinarily <term>spheroidal</term><note>original: "sphäroidisch"</note> or <term>orange-shaped</term><note>original: "pomeranzenförmig." A "Pomeranze" is a bitter orange; this was a common 18th-century scientific analogy for an oblate spheroid.</note>. It becomes, however, even more spheroidal from time to time.

This phenomenon is compared to the movement of seawater on Earth and confirmed by astronomical observations of Jupiter's flattened shape.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the astronomical discussion from page 422, moving from the rotation of Jupiter to the specific physical characteristics and age of Saturn, as well as the author's theory on the formation of Saturn's rings.</meta>

...of man through God.

How fast Saturn rotates on its axis cannot be known, because it is too far away from us and receives too little light from the Sun for valleys and mountains to be seen on it through a telescope—as they can be on most other planets—to allow one to infer the duration of its rotation from their progression. It is probable, however, that it does rotate, and indeed very quickly. Moreover, it is likely a hundred million years older than Jupiter, because it stands nearly twice as far from the Sun as the latter; the Sun, as we have seen above, required approximately two hundred million years for the birthing of all the planets. One can reasonably assume that <term>Caelus</term> <note>original: "Cölus." In historical astronomy, the name of the Roman sky god Caelus was often used for the planet we now call Uranus.</note> and Saturn were ejected or formed in the first hundred million years, while Jupiter, Mars, Earth, Venus, and Mercury, by contrast, were formed in the second hundred million years.

Because of Saturn's long existence, and because of its likely very rapid <term>centrifugal force</term> <note>original: "Dreheschwung," literally "rotational swing."</note>, its fluid materials were once so greatly swollen around its equator that their momentum overcame their gravity, tearing them away from the planet all around and hurling them high into the height with equal force at every point. Near to the planets, it is warmer than further away from them due to the manifold <term>reverberation</term> <note>original: "Reperkussion," a historical term for the reflection or bouncing back of light or heat rays.</note> of solar rays; further away, the solar rays cannot reflect but merely travel straight ahead. Experience on the high mountains of our Earth teaches us this, and it would undoubtedly teach us the same on other planets if we could make observations upon them. -># Thoughts on the Destination<-

...clumped together, but was instead ejected whole and all at once from the burning globe of the Earth.

In much the same way as our Moon, the moons of Saturn and Jupiter likely also appear, since they all possess little mass and, consequently, can have little air and few liquid materials similar to our water. But let us now cast another glance at the primary planets themselves.

Jupiter has a circumference forty times larger than our Earthly globe. Nevertheless, it rotates once on its axis within nine hours, whereas our Earthly globe requires twenty-four hours to complete its <term>rotation</term> <note>original: "Rotazion."</note> once. Therefore, Jupiter rotates over a hundred times faster than the Earthly globe. <note>The author calculates this by comparing the linear speed at the equator: since Jupiter is forty times larger but rotates in less than half the time, its surface moves significantly faster than Earth's.</note>

Because of this rotation, our Earthly globe is even now gradually becoming thicker between the <term>tropics</term> <note>original: "Wendekreisen," literally "turning circles."</note>, while it sinks by an equal amount near the poles. By virtue of the <term>centrifugal force</term> <note>original: "Dreheschwung," literally "rotational swing," a historical term for the force that pushes matter away from the center of a rotating body.</note>, which is greatest between the tropics and smallest near the poles, the seawater rises from both poles toward the equator; there, the sea must swell between the tropics and gradually flood flat lands, because not as much flows back as streams there from both sides. Since Jupiter now rotates a hundred times faster than the Earth, the centrifugal force near its equator must be a hundred times greater than that of our Earth at its equator. Consequently, Jupiter must swell far more at its equator than our Earthly globe; and astronomical measurements indeed confirm that this planet is extraordinarily <term>spheroidal</term> <note>original: "sphäroidisch."</note> or orange-shaped. Moreover, from time to time, it becomes even more spheroidal.

### ...of Man through God.

How swiftly **Saturn** rotates upon its **axis** cannot be known, because it is too far removed from us and receives too little **light** from the **Sun** for us to be able to see **valleys** and **mountains** upon it through the **telescope**—as we can on most of the other **planets**. We are therefore unable to use the **advancement** of such features to conclude the **duration** of its **rotation**. **Probably**, however, it does rotate, and indeed very swiftly. Furthermore, it is likely a hundred million **years** older than **Jupiter**, because it stands nearly twice as far from the **Sun** as the latter; the Sun, as we have seen above, required approximately two hundred million **years** for the **birthing** <note>original: "Ausgeburth," here meaning the ejection or formation of celestial bodies from the solar mass.</note> of all the **planets**. One can reasonably assume that **Coius** <note>Likely referring to Coelus, an early name associated with the planet Uranus, discovered in 1781.</note> and **Saturn** were ejected or formed in the first **hundred million years**, while **Jupiter**, **Mars**, **Earth**, **Venus**, and **Mercury**, by contrast, were formed in the second **hundred million**.

# ...of Man through God.

...of our Earth, the orbits of the same would undoubtedly, as mentioned, soon be noticeably displaced.

Thus our planetary system is clearly constructed mathematically, and arranged purposefully with infinite wisdom. According to mathematical principles it was formed, and according to mathematical principles it is governed and maintained. The smallest particle of it belongs to the purpose of the whole; the whole, on the other hand, harmonizes again with each of its parts. It is often compared to a clock, but the comparison does not fit. Wheels remain wheels, and mainsprings remain mainsprings, even if no clock is made from them. In our planetary system, however, no body can exist for itself alone: they must necessarily all remain in connection at the same time, keep one another in balance, and support one another. They all collapse as soon as one collapses, and every individual one falls back into its <term>chaos</term> <note>The author uses "chaos" here in the classical sense: a state of formless matter before the universe was ordered.</note> as soon as all the others go to ruin. Only other planetary systems can perhaps be shattered without harming our own.

Can a person, then—unless asserting something against their own better judgment and without any reason—imagine that such a purposeful work, arranged according to the strictest mathematical rules, could have arisen by chance through blind accident <note>original: "blindes Ohngefähr." This refers to the concept of Epicurean "randomness" which Enlightenment thinkers often argued against.</note>? No, no one can, unless they were to imagine this themselves by accident, and without any intention, or without any reason. How great, how glorious, how wise, how powerful must that incomprehensible Being be, therefore, who has prepared not only this <term>machine</term> <note>The "World Machine" was a common Enlightenment metaphor for the universe as a self-regulating, designed system.</note> of our planets, but also infinitely many others so unimaginably skillfully, and still prepares and governs them? How clearly is the unspeakable love and goodness of this Being, whose name is God, shown in the

# ...of mankind through God.

...descriptions of the comet of 1745 <note>The Great Comet of 1744, often referred to as Comet de Chéseaux, was also observed into 1745. They also appear in Fontenelle’s *On the Plurality of Worlds* <note>original: "sur la pluralité des mondes." A famous 1686 work by Bernard le Bovier de Fontenelle that popularized Cartesian astronomy.</note>, and in the *Cosmological Conversations*, though not as beautifully as in the original work itself.

Comets are nothing more than loose clumps of highly refined **phosphoric matter**, which are expanded by the light of the sun the closer they approach it, and pull themselves together more densely the further they move away from it. When they come as close to the sun as Venus or even Mercury, they seem, as it were, to break apart into pieces, which nevertheless always maintain a specific shape and remain connected to one another. Sunlight seems, in a sense, to tear away large masses of this matter from their edges all around and carry it along in straight directions. The brightest part of these is called the **nucleus** <term>nucleus</term> <note>The author uses the term "Kern." In 18th-century astronomy, the nucleus was often thought to be a dense collection of vapors rather than a solid rocky body.</note>, which evidently consists of nothing but phosphorescent vapors and only appears brighter because of its greater density than that which is located around and behind the nucleus. It is from this very nucleus that the solar rays tear away the outermost loose matter and carry it with them, often many millions of miles into the heavens, to form the so-called **comet tail**. Consequently, this tail must necessarily appear dense and narrow near the nucleus, but thin or loose and wide far behind it; for the aforementioned vapors spread out further the further the solar rays carry them away from the nucleus.

### Thoughts on the Calling

...density, and they have a far more elongated shape than the planetary orbits.

These wonderful clumps of vapor <note>original: "Dunstklumpen." The author describes comets not as solid rocks, but as loose, atmospheric-like masses.</note>, which often far exceed the entire Earth in size, but are often also much smaller than it, traverse the planes of the planetary orbits in every possible direction. They often fly past us in the vicinity of our terrestrial globe—that is, at a distance of barely a few million miles—and sink deep down toward the sun, where they swing around close behind it with increased speed, but then return again to where they came from, gradually disappearing from our earthly eyes again, and perhaps go far beyond the orbits of all planets, only to return anew and begin their orbit once more, which for most lasts over a hundred years.

Since the year 837 of our era <note>The year 837 AD saw a particularly spectacular appearance of Halley’s Comet, which came exceptionally close to Earth.</note>, sixty-five such different **phosphorus balls** <note>original: "Phosphorusbälle." In this period, "phosphorus" referred generally to substances that glowed with a "cold" light, reflecting the theory that comets were made of self-luminous, phosphoric matter.</note> have been observed. Some of these have indeed already been back several times since then; but perhaps there are many that need millennia to complete their orbits once. Often they also come in from the deep heavens beside the sun and swing past it, only to run out again on the other side beside it without us seeing them, because in this case they appear to the Earth only during the day, and consequently are obscured for us by the sun’s rays, like all other stars. Since only sixty-five such different white balls of vapor, which belong to our solar system, have been observed during nine hundred years, their number must be even more considerable, because surely many of them swing around the sun without ever being noticed by the inhabitants of the Earth.

Hevel <note>Johannes Hevelius (1611–1687), a Polish astronomer famous for his detailed lunar maps and star catalogs.</note> observed one between the years 1670 and 1672 at the beak of the Swan <note>The constellation Cygnus.</note>. On the contrary, various stars that are recorded in the star catalogs of the ancient Greek astronomers have already vanished and are no longer to be seen. Such strange celestial phenomena undeniably teach us that even now, suns and worlds must be in the process of forming, just as others are approaching their destruction. Professor Mayer of Mannheim <note>Christian Mayer (1719–1783), a Jesuit astronomer who was one of the first to study binary stars.</note> also claims to have seen fiery wandering stars <term>Wandelsterne|An archaic term for planets, from the German 'wandering stars.'</term> through a very good achromatic telescope, which swing around their suns just as our planets move around our sun. If these observations are correct, they once again clearly teach us that these fiery planets of certain solar stars are younger than our planets and, consequently, have not yet burned out; for our planets also initially represented small suns whirling around their primary sun when their surfaces were still entirely dotted with burning volcanoes. There are also a few solar stars that shine sometimes brightly and sometimes weakly. One stands at the breast of the Swan and completes its light cycle once every 405 days. The other stands in the Whale <note>The constellation Cetus; the star described is Mira, the first periodic variable star discovered.</note> and reaches its greatest clarity every 334 days. They are commonly called miracle stars <term>Wundersterne|A historical term for variable stars whose brightness fluctuates over time.</term>. Probably, they rotate once on their axes during the cited times and burn more strongly on one half of their surface than the other. Therefore, they must certainly appear now bright, now dim, now large, and now small.

# Thoughts on the Destiny of Man

### [The Origin of the Earth]

From this it is clear how little one should, following Moses <note>The author refers to the Biblical account of creation in Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note>, make the Earth the primary object of Creation, since it is so small—nearly nothing—in comparison to all other celestial bodies. Indisputably, the ancient Egyptians, along with Moses, established the week (or the duration of a lunar quarter) as the "period of creation" because it was one of the oldest time periods known, and because they counted exactly seven planets. They held the highest of these planets to be the supreme God, by whom all the others had been begotten.

But we now wish to leave the heavens and descend to the Earth.

The Earth was thus ejected from the Sun in fragments. Consequently, it could not be smooth or level, but had to acquire immense humps and bumps upon its surface. This is because the aforementioned burning fragments were themselves undoubtedly quite compact and jagged when the Creator cast them together to form this terrestrial globe. Thus arose the high basalt peaks <note>The author is likely referencing 18th-century "Plutonist" theories, which argued that rocks like basalt were formed through volcanic heat rather than settling in water.</note>, which were originally much higher than they are now, because weathering over so many millennia has dissolved and washed away a very large portion of them. Upon these primordial basalt and slag peaks, new shells of volcanic matter were immediately deposited in layers, as we shall hear more about shortly.

Air indeed already surrounded the burning terrestrial globe when the hand of its Great Architect <term>Werkmeister|Literally "Master Workman." In the 18th century, this was a common way to describe God as a rational craftsman or engineer of the universe.</term> cast it down from the Sun; but the mighty heat, which the globe spread for many miles around itself, expanded the air immensely. This heat by no means allowed the water—which was mixed with the air in the form of vapor—to condense and collect together into seas or lakes
