### of man through God ###

**Reason** <note>original: "Vernunft". In the philosophical context of the 18th century, Reason was considered the highest human faculty, capable of grasping universal truths.</note> and **understanding** <note>original: "Verstand". This refers to the faculty of logic and empirical processing.</note> could not be taken into account here at all: for understanding and reason rely on grounds that are generally recognized as true as soon as they are seen in full light, and no person who asserts such a thing <note>Meaning: anyone who asserts that the world is the product of chance.</note> can build their proof on such grounds. If he asserted his proposition, he himself would be a mere **accident**. <note>original: "Ohngefähr". This archaic term denotes "blind chance" or a "haphazard occurrence." The author argues that if the universe is an accident, then the person arguing it—and the argument itself—must also be meaningless accidents.</note> Were he himself a mere accident, so too would be the proposition he asserted, because an accident cannot possibly produce something purposeful or something deliberate. Therefore, one could not turn his proposition into a constant truth, because truth is unchangeable and constant, whereas accident, by contrast, is now one way, now another.

Thus, a Being must necessarily exist who is the sum of all wisdom, all knowledge, all sciences, and all truths that are found in the infinite whole, and according to which the whole—of which we, as finite beings, certainly have no complete concept—as well as its individual parts, are prepared and arranged. **God** is His name. Therefore, a God is necessary.

Now, however, the world—at least in its variety and extension—is beyond contradiction infinite: for neither understanding nor the senses show us an end to it. Therefore, God is infinitely wise, infinitely true, infinitely understanding, infinitely good, infinitely just, infinitely loving, and so forth.

Now the question arises: Is God perhaps that very force which has worked and maintains the world as a whole, as well as in all its parts? Or, is He a distinct Being from whom the force, with which the world as it were maintains itself, has proceeded?

# Thoughts on Destiny #
<note>original: "Bestimmung". In 18th-century German philosophy, this term refers to "vocation," "destination," or the "ultimate purpose" of a being.</note>

Usually, the latter is asserted. It is said: God created the power and placed it into nature at the time of **Creation**, so that we can now see and feel its effects; but He Himself is entirely distinct from this power. It is further said: In the beginning, God prescribed to nature all the specific and manifold **laws** <note>original: "Gesätze", an archaic spelling of "Gesetze".</note> which we now see being followed; for He Himself no longer acts directly, but instead lets nature act on its own, just as a **clockmaker** leaves his clock to run by itself once it is finished. <note>The "Clockmaker" analogy is a hallmark of Deism, suggesting a rational but distant God who does not intervene in the natural order.</note>

One concludes in the following manner: Nothing in the world arises of itself. I am. But I have come from my **parents**. My parents from theirs. These again from theirs, and so on. Thus, I finally come to parents who did not arise in the ordinary way, but came directly from God. So it is with all things. Therefore, the world also did not arise from its own powers, but was created by a particular Being who stands in no necessary connection with it; for the world is also not eternal and unchangeable, because its parts are destructible and changeable. God has the ground of His **existence** within Himself, and is eternal, unchangeable, and necessary. The world, on the other hand, has the ground of its existence outside of itself—namely, in God—and is transient, changeable, and accidental. <term>Accidental</term> <note>original: "zufällig". In philosophical logic, this refers to "contingent" things—beings that could possibly not exist, unlike a "necessary" being.</note> Thus, God is indeed distinct from the world.

However, in these conclusions, two **fallacies** <note>original: "Fallazien", from the Latin "fallacia".</note> clearly lie hidden.

The first fallacy consists in this: that one regards the world merely as the connection of bodies and **matter**...

After all, we have not yet observed the forces themselves, but only their **effects**. How can we then conclude that a force is not acting simply because we perceive no effect? Where no bodies or materials are present, we do not perceive the effect of **gravity** <note>original: "Schwere", literally "heaviness." The author is using the Newtonian concept of universal gravitation to argue for the existence of invisible, constant forces.</note>. But would it be correct to conclude that no gravity exists or acts there? Not at all. One need only bring bodies or materials to that place, and one will instantly perceive the effect; for gravity acts and is constantly active everywhere around our globe, and thus even where we do not perceive its effect. Just as gravity always acts, even if it finds no materials, so too can other forces always act, even though we often do not notice their effects outside of matter.

Yes, it is said, forces belong to the **essence** of materials, and are nothing more as soon as one destroys the bodies and materials in which they are located! They change as the essence of the materials and bodies is changed!

->### Thoughts on Determination ###<-

Therefore, one can proceed much more briefly and say without hesitation: The **force** <note>In 18th-century philosophy, "Kraft" (force or power) was often viewed as the bridge between the spiritual and material worlds—the active agency through which God influences the physical universe.</note> which created and maintains the world is itself independent, eternal, immutable, wise, good, almighty, and is called **God**. For if nothing at all can have the ground of its existence in itself, then God Himself cannot have it in Himself either.

Now, however, a **being** must necessarily have the ground of its existence in itself, as has been clearly demonstrated above: consequently, this **being** must either be the **force** itself that formed and maintains the world, or there must exist yet another distinct **being** that created and maintains this **force** itself. But as we have seen, there are no grounds at all for assuming the latter. Rather, there are reasons to assert the former, because one should not assume a distinct being without necessity, nor pile **being** upon **being** when a single one is sufficient. <note>This is a reference to the principle of parsimony, or "Occam’s Razor," which suggests that the simplest explanation with the fewest moving parts is usually the correct one.</note> Whoever wished to pile such beings upon one another would fall into exactly the same error that many of our **physicers** <note>The term "Physiker" here refers to natural philosophers who studied the physical laws of the universe.</note> fall into when they attempt to explain **gravity**. Would one not do much better to accept **gravity** itself for what it is—as a self-acting **force**—and not pile new causes upon new causes...

# Thoughts on Destiny
<meta>catchword: How</meta>

...being, who is life, power, and effectiveness itself, can be inactive?

That He should only work at certain times, and at other times not work at all, is also difficult to imagine; for in such a case, nothing in the world could occur according to fixed **laws** <term>Gesätze: An archaic spelling of "Gesetze." In this context, it refers to the immutable laws of nature established by divine wisdom.</term> and rules. One would have to expect at every moment that God might, now here and then elsewhere, obstruct the course of nature and not allow it to proceed according to the prescribed rules. From this, however, one would have to conclude that the rules themselves were not universally correct or applicable. Furthermore, one would have to conclude that God could not be infinitely wise and all-knowing, because He did not adapt the laws from the very beginning to all the events that were meant to be governed by them. Such a world would therefore undoubtedly be a very imperfect thing, a mere **patchwork** <note>original: "Flickwerk." But who can claim this with any probability, unless they thoughtlessly imagine God to be like a human being, who indeed always finds much to improve upon in his own works?

God, therefore, works constantly. God is thus the cause of all effects that we perceive in the world. **God works all in all.** **God is all in all.** <note>These are direct references to the New Testament, specifically 1 Corinthians 12:6 ("it is the same God who works all in all") and 15:28 ("that God may be all in all").</note> These words are even the words of Scripture. # The Governance of Man by God

->Perhaps it is imagined that in this way God is made the author of evil.<-

First, however, one must consider that what is absolutely impossible cannot be made possible, much less actual, even by God Himself. The **absolute best** for every individual must therefore have been simply impossible in itself, if truly real evil exists in the world. If everything in the world were meant to be absolutely good and perfect, then everything would have to equal God Himself in perfection and goodness. But this was simply impossible. If it had been possible, God would have had to be able to create Himself, or other gods who were perfectly equal to Him; and thus He would no longer be the absolutely necessary **highest being** <note>original: "höchste Wesen." In 18th-century philosophy, this refers to the *ens realissimum*, the most real and necessary being who is the ground of all existence.</note>; for He would not need to have His foundation within Himself, because other highest beings could have begotten Him. One sees, then, what absurdities one falls into when asserting the possibility of a world in which every individual is absolutely good and knows nothing of any evil. 

Thus, it follows from this reason alone that God—or the universal **world-force** <term>Weltkraft: A term often used by Enlightenment thinkers to bridge the gap between theology and physics, describing God not as a distant ruler, but as the active energy sustaining the laws of nature.</term>—must by no means be called the author of evil. This evil is absolutely necessary in every possible world because it is impossible for the creatures to be equal to the Creator, or for the individual parts to be equal to the whole. But He is certainly the author of good: for He has created everything and still does everything now; consequently, He also does what is good. Therefore, all good necessarily comes from Him.

Secondly, one does not even know how to draw the boundaries between good and evil—I am speaking here, as is easy to see, entirely of **physical evil** and **physical good** <note>The author distinguishes between "moral evil" (sin) and "physical evil" (suffering, decay, or natural disasters). The argument here is that humans lack the perspective to know if a physical hardship is actually harmful in the long run.</note>—one does not even know, I say, what is truly good or harmful to us?

But in respect to the whole, there is no evil in the world. It is abundantly supplied with all the good that is ever possible.

# Thoughts on the Vocation

<meta>catchword: not</meta>

...must? Thus, one also cannot say that mathematicians are able to measure God, if He is the universal **world-force** <term>world-force: "Weltkraft," the animating divine energy or power that sustains the physical laws of the universe.</term>. Yet, will one not nonetheless deny that many of His effects are measurable, since He has, in all instances, worked everything in the world?

->We come now to the **vocation** of man.<-
<note>"Bestimmung" (vocation/destiny) refers to the inherent purpose or goal for which a human being is created.</note>

Man thinks and feels. He can think extensively and feel strongly if he practices these actions of his. With his understanding, he can even draw near to God; that is, he can elevate himself to knowledge that belongs to the Highest Himself, save that he can never reach the highest degrees of the perfection of such knowledge. Thoughts and feelings are effects that necessarily require a certain cause, which we call **force** <term>force: "Kraft," a fundamental philosophical concept of the era (associated with Leibniz and Wolff) referring to the inherent power of a substance to produce change.</term>. This force, however, bears the name of the **soul**, or the **human spirit**, which must necessarily be a distinct being that is entirely different from the body.

If force in general belonged to the essence of matter, then the force with which the ball moves on the billiard table <note>The "billiard ball" was a common 18th-century philosophical illustration used to explain causality and the transfer of motion, most famously by David Hume.</note> would also have to belong to its essence, and it could not impart this force to another without at the same time imparting its essence to it. Whoever might then wish to claim that one ball, according to its essence, passes into the other upon contact, would undoubtedly be laughed at by all billiard players, because then the marks <note>original: "Marken." Referring to the small spots or numbers used to distinguish one ball from another.</note> with which one is accustomed to designate the balls would have to pass over at the same time. Thus, the billiard players would be at odds every moment regarding their balls. For whoever does not find this example illuminating enough, let him consider here again that even **gravity** <term>gravity: "Schwere," referring to the weight or gravitational pull acting on an object.</term> cannot belong to the essence of matter, as we have already seen above. If gravity were essentially inherent to matter, then gravity would always have to remain unchangeable in matter; that is, matter would have to be equally heavy everywhere, regardless of whether one carried it here or there. But it does not do this. Rather, it is known that all matter between the **tropics** <term>tropics: "Wendekreise," the regions of the Earth surrounding the Equator.</term> is lighter than between other parallels that lie closer toward the poles; and at an altitude of eight hundred and sixty miles <note>A "German mile" in the 18th century was significantly longer than a modern English mile, usually measuring about 7.5 kilometers.</note> above the Earth's surface, all matter is four times less heavy than near the Earth's surface itself. # Thoughts on Destiny

...the force through which changes in matter and bodies are brought about is not essential to matter and bodies; rather, these forces are independent substances in their own right, and they reveal themselves to us only through their effects upon matter. A stone that is unsupported falls toward the center of the earth in our world because **gravity** <term>gravity: "Schwere," here referring to the gravitational force that acts upon weight.</term> drives it there. This gravity is not matter, but merely **force**, which certainly never shows us its essence, but only its effects. The billiard ball to which I give a strike moves forward in the given direction only because I drive it there. I, however, am not matter, but merely **force**, and therefore I cannot, of course, perceive my own essence, but only my effects. My body does not belong to my essence, not to the **"I."** <term>the "I": "Das Ich," referring to the self or the soul as a thinking, acting subject.</term> It is only my tool with which I am to act upon earthly bodies. The **"I"** is merely myself. I see the paper upon which I write only because it is illuminated by **light**. Light itself, however, is not matter, but mere **force**, which reveals itself to us through and in matter.

**Newton** and **Euler** <note>Sir Isaac Newton (1642–1727) and Leonhard Euler (1707–1783) were two of the most influential scientists of the era. Their differing views on the nature of light—Newton favoring particles and Euler favoring waves—were a central debate in 18th-century physics.</note> admittedly say that light is matter. The latter [Euler] considers it to be **aether vibrations**, and the former [Newton] considers it to be a highly refined **outflow** <note>original: "Ausfluß." This refers to Newton’s corpuscular theory, which posited that light consisted of tiny particles emitted from source bodies.</note> of luminous bodies. However, both hypotheses are subject to irreconcilable contradictions—though Euler’s are subjected to far more than Newton’s. Euler assumes that light cannot be an outflow of luminous matter because the sun would necessarily have to become smaller and smaller in this way, which, however, does not happen. For this reason, he devises the "aether vibrations." But one need only consider that all the suns would send each other their outflows if light were truly matter and Newton’s hypothesis were well-founded.

Why then would one not rather consider light itself to be this force, since the hypotheses that one places between the light and its ultimate cause neither expand our knowledge nor bring us a hair's breadth closer to the truth?

# Thoughts on the Destination [of Man]

That a point is neither long nor wide and has no parts—one does not learn that through the help of the senses, does one? That a line has no width, and a plane has no height or thickness—one does not know this from experience? <note>These geometric definitions are classic examples used by Enlightenment thinkers to prove the existence of "a priori" knowledge—truths that are independent of sensory experience.</note> From where, then, does one know these and many other such truths, if the concepts of them do not lie within us from the beginning? Therefore, I must have felt and recognized them before I received these tools for perceiving the physical world; for in this life, I did not receive them. Consequently, one cannot claim that before birth one neither thought nor felt. One simply did not feel the things that one commonly feels now, and did not reflect upon them.

But why do we think and feel strongly and clearly when the body is healthy and has reached its full growth? Why are we childish in our thinking and feeling in childhood, just as in old age?

It is because we perceive only our effects, but never ourselves—that is, because we can only feel and judge the effect of the <term>Kraft: force or power; here referring to the soul as an active, immaterial energy</term>, never the force itself. In this life, however, we usually notice the effects of forces only on matter and bodies. If these are changed by an external force or even by the internal force itself, then...

...himself, however, he certainly never becomes His equal, for He is infinitely perfect. He only approaches God infinitely, like the <term>hyperbola</term> <note>A mathematical curve that constantly approaches a straight line but never actually touches it.</note> to its <term>asymptote</term>, or like the <term>integrals</term> and <term>differentials</term> of the circle approach the true <term>quadrature</term> <note>original: "Quadratinhalte"; the mathematical process of calculating the area of a circle. Whether after this life he will also act upon matter, as he does now, or whether he is merely to come into connection with other beings like himself, I cannot decide: but act, or think and feel, he certainly will, for in these consists his essence.

God has, moreover, ordered the entire world so incomprehensibly beautiful, so good, so magnificent, and so wise, for the sole purpose that all creatures may become as happy as is ever possible, and may progress from higher to higher perfections. How then can He exempt man alone from this, since man possesses within himself the capacity for eternal life, for the eternal growth of his perfection?

If man, along with his tools—I mean his sensory organs—were killed and made entirely ineffective at once, he would undeniably be the most miserable creature on earth; God would have imprinted His <term>image</term> <note>The *Imago Dei*, the theological concept that humans are created in God’s likeness, specifically through the faculty of reason.</note>—I mean <term>Reason</term>—upon him merely to make him all the more unhappy through it.

The irrational animal knows no happiness but the life of its body, its fodder, and its reproductive drive. Perhaps it does not even have actual knowledge of these things. Nevertheless, it flees death and hunger. Man, through his reason, raises himself infinitely above the cattle, and even dares to penetrate into the secrets of the <term>Godhead</term>, into the laws by which He governs the world. And yet this being is meant to wish for perfection in vain? Could God have imprinted this holy wish so deeply within him in flaming characters all in vain? # Thoughts on Human Destiny

...sooner or later, he must feel and recognize the state of lowliness <note>original: "Niedrigkeit"; refers here to a diminished moral or spiritual condition.</note> brought upon himself by his own fault. By his very nature, he is destined to feel and to know; however, in this life, he often perceives and feels things incorrectly or in a distorted way. This happens because the body seems closer to him than he is to himself, and because it is always easier to see, feel, and judge what lies outside of us than what lies within. But when nothing outside of me remains upon which I can fix my attention, then I must converse with myself; then I know and feel myself more truly.

Growth in the knowledge of truth and growth in the knowledge of God is, therefore, the destiny of man. It is eternal <term>happiness</term> <note>original: "Glückseligkeit"; a state of supreme bliss, blessedness, or well-being that was a central goal of Enlightenment philosophy.</note> and the natural and necessary consequence of his actions and deeds. Conversely, the decline of the knowledge of truth and the decline of the knowledge of God is not the destiny of man; it is unhappiness, and likewise the natural and necessary consequence of his actions and deeds.

Thus, God does not make the wise and the good happy simply because He wills it; rather, the wise and good person makes himself happy because his happiness is the necessary and natural result of his actions. Similarly, God does not make the fool and the wicked person unhappy out of mere caprice, like a stubborn <term>despot</term> <note>An absolute ruler who governs according to their own whims rather than laws; the author argues that God is governed by reason and natural law, not whim.</note>. Instead, the fool and the wicked man make themselves unhappy because their unhappiness—that is, the consciousness of the decline they have brought upon themselves—is the necessary and natural consequence of their own actions and deeds.

### ...of Man through God.

Use your sense organs primarily for the knowledge of creation, so that you may recognize God, or the truth: for God is truth, and knowledge of the truth is that which raises you from stage to stage toward the perfection that makes you happy both temporally and eternally—You are, by your very nature, destined for growth in perfection.

Revere God in the highest degree! That is: Strive to imitate God in all your actions as much as is ever possible, and to deal with your fellow creatures in a way that is just, kind, wise, loving, tolerant, benevolent, and forgiving—God wills the highest possible well-being of the whole, and promotes it—If you wish to imitate Him, and be happy yourself, then you must likewise will the well-being of the whole, and promote it.

Seek to increase your knowledge in every possible way—Sharpen your <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "Verstand"; in 18th-century philosophy, this refers to the capacity for logical reasoning and the processing of sensory information.</note> as much as you ever can, and derive truths from vast quantities of concepts—You shall test everything, and keep only that which is good—You shall promote the well-being of the whole, and not your own if the whole suffers because of it, for otherwise you make yourself unhappy while believing you are making yourself happy—You are a part of the whole—if the whole suffers, then all its parts suffer as well, and consequently you yourself suffer if you offend the whole merely to promote your own well-being—But you cannot comprehend all of this if you have a limited intellect: for the true promotion of the well-being of the whole requires a very expanded intellect, which is called <term>wisdom</term> <note>original: "Weisheit"; here defined as the practical application of a highly developed intellect toward the universal good.</note>—Without wisdom, one often harms the whole while <insert>believing</insert> <note>The text transitions here to the catchword "glaubt" (believes) on the following page.</note> one is promoting its well-being.

# Thoughts on Destiny

He must, sooner or later, feel and recognize the <term>debasement</term> <note>original: "Niedrigkeit"; refers here to a state of spiritual or moral lowliness or a loss of dignity brought about by one's own choices.</note> brought upon himself through his own fault: for he is, by his very nature, destined for feeling and knowing, only that in this life he often perceives and feels in a perverted or distorted way, because the body seems closer to him than he is to himself, and because it is always easier to see, feel, and judge that which lies outside us than that which lies within us—But when nothing more lies outside me upon which I can fix my gaze, then I must converse with myself; then I recognize and feel myself more truly.

If you live in a land where <term>religious ceremonies</term> <note>original: "Religionszeremonien"; the outward rituals and traditional rites of a faith.</note> are held as laws, then follow them, even if you are <term>philosopher</term> <note>original: "Philosoph"; an enlightened or rational thinker.</note> enough to see that they are mere ceremonies and basically of no use to the philosopher. Were you not to follow them, you would be cast out from the community of your fellow citizens. You would then no longer be a member of public society, would have to forfeit all the advantages that come to you as a <term>citizen of the state</term> <note>original: "Staatsbürger"; a member of a political community with shared rights and duties.</note>, and consequently could no longer do as much good as before. You would thus become imperfect and unhappy, which would again be contrary to your destiny. Therefore, you must follow these religious ceremonies.

If you are a <term>master</term> <note>original: "Herr"; here referring to any person in a position of authority, such as an employer or landlord.</note>, then regard your subordinates as parts of the <term>Whole</term> <note>original: "das Ganze"; the interconnected system of humanity and the divine order.</note> to which you also belong. Be wise, therefore, and treat these parts of the Whole—your subordinates—in such a way that the welfare of the Whole, and thus your own welfare, is promoted. Put yourself often in their place, and examine how you would wish to be treated by your master. Treat them exactly as you would wish to be treated yourself. If you treat them poorly, you offend the Whole, of which you are also a part, and consequently degrade yourself. In doing so, you act against your destiny and make yourself unhappier than you are meant to be.

If you are a <term>servant</term> <note>original: "Diener"; one who is in a position of service or subordination.</note>, then follow the commands of your master accurately and punctually. If you do not do this, you will fall into punishment and hardship. Punishment and hardship, however, are contrary to the <term>growth of your perfection</term> <note>original: "Wachsthume deiner Vollkommenheit"; the continuous process of moral and spiritual refinement.</note>, and necessarily have an eternal influence

### Thoughts on Destiny

...upon yourself, because the growth of your well-being in eternity remains behind by as much as you have hindered it here, or perhaps even driven it back.

If you are **spouses**, then observe perfectly equal duties toward one another—you are both, as it were, only one, and consequently have no need at all to ask whether you should mutually make each other as happy as ever possible—if you do not do this, you act against your <term>destiny</term> <note>original: "Bestimmung"; the inherent purpose or "vocation" of a human being to progress toward a higher moral and spiritual state.</note>—you make yourselves unhappier than you could and should be—evil that arises from this is a necessary natural consequence of your conduct toward one another, and has an eternal influence on your **bliss** <note>original: "Glückseligkeit"; a state of supreme, often spiritual, happiness or beatitude.</note>—But if one, due to physical causes, cannot fulfill the duties owed to the other as a spouse, then you both, as is easy to see, cannot be spouses, and merely have the duty to observe the mutual obligations of human beings toward one another.

If you live outside of **marriage**, live chastely and modestly. Preserve your health with foods that serve only to maintain your sensory organs and do not incite other limbs to **lust** <note>original: "Wollust"; physical pleasure or carnal desire, often viewed with suspicion in Enlightenment moral philosophy.</note>—guard yourself against dissolute excesses through **industriousness** <note>original: "Arbeitsamkeit"; the virtue of being hard-working and productive.</note>—think only of your affairs—learn diligently and work diligently, so that you may acquire the means and necessities required for the **state of marriage**, and then take a wife—you will see that you will be happy and become ever happier through this—if you do not wish to follow these duties toward yourself, but wallow in the mire of **fornication** <note>original: "Unzucht"; sexual conduct deemed immoral or outside of social norms.</note>, seduce innocence, or even satisfy your lustful desires, incited with diligence, in an unnatural, not even beastly manner, then you act directly contrary to your destiny in the most irrational way,

### [The Destiny] of Man through God.

...you destroy not only your body, but often also make your **fellow human beings** unhappy; indeed, you even ruin your **offspring** if you commit unnatural **excesses** <note>original: "Ausschweifungen"; refers to lack of moderation or debauchery, particularly in a sexual or physical context.</note>—How much do you not thereby hinder the growth of the **perfection** of the whole? How much do you degrade yourself through this? How heavily must the consciousness of these evil actions weigh upon you when, sooner or later, you come to the realization of them? Consider that the **generation** <note>original: "Erzeugung"; the act of procreation or bringing forth life.</note> of new **sensory organs** is the work of the wise **Creator**, who uses you as an instrument to lead beings toward the growth of their perfection! Consider that reproduction is the most sublime and most important business of nature, which belongs to the **destiny** <note>original: "Bestimmung"; the inherent purpose or vocation of a human being.</note> of beings! Do you wish to oppose this noble business, or rather, its great purpose, so cruelly? To disturb the progress of beings toward a higher perfection? To ruin your own offspring? How? Can one who causes ruin also be happy?

**Love your neighbor as yourself**—Always put yourself in his place whenever you have a matter with him, and examine how you would wish to be treated by him—Then you also treat him as you desire that he should treat you—Do not search for faults in your neighbor, but in yourself—Improve your own faults first, then rebuke the failings of others in general, not individual people—You would otherwise bring upon yourself vexation that would be contrary to your destiny—But you are made to be happy and to become ever happier.

If you have already done evil, then seek [to redress] the harm you have caused through all the more good **deeds—**

# Thoughts on [Man's] Destiny

...to make things right again—Through mere prayer for forgiveness of sins, nothing is made right again. What has been made evil through evil deeds, that must be made right again through good deeds—Can you not do that? All the worse for you! Therefore, be wise, and commit no evil!

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore, honor God above all! That is: Be wise! Seek to increase your happiness <note>original: "Glückseligkeit"; a state of supreme well-being or blessedness.</note>! Promote the well-being of the whole with all your strength! Love your neighbor as yourself! Learn to recognize God from his works: for this knowledge <note>original: "Erkanntniß"; an experiential or intellectual realization.</note> of God is wisdom! This wisdom alone makes you happy, makes you fit to promote the well-being of the whole, just as you ought.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Whoever follows these principles will undoubtedly grow in perfection eternally. But whoever follows the opposite will unfailingly remain eternally behind in their growth in perfection. Happiness follows necessarily and naturally from good actions: unhappiness follows just as naturally and necessarily from evil deeds—not out of any caprice <note>original: "Kaprize"; an arbitrary whim or fancy.</note> of the Lord of the Worlds, because he is far too great, far too exalted, and far too holy to be offended <note>The author suggests that God is above human emotion; therefore, "punishment" is not divine anger, but a natural consequence of one's own actions.</note>.

# Conclusion

->Eternal, loving God! Father and Sustainer of the worlds!<-

> Hear my prayer! You know my heart! You know how often, how fervently, how urgently I have pleaded with You to lead me to the recognition <note>original: "Erkenntniß"; a deep, experiential understanding or realization.</note> of the truth! Only You know the anguish, the pain, that doubts about the doctrines—which people take for Your immediate will—have caused me! You alone know that I never doubted out of frivolity, nor wished to scrutinize and investigate generally prevailing opinions, passed down to us from of old and held as Your word, out of a penchant for evil! Much that is presented as Your own commands, as Your own words, I now recognize as human work <note>original: "Menschenwerk"; something constructed by humans rather than divinely ordained.</note>, as poetry and fables. Holy, gracious Father, forgive me if I am in error! Perhaps I am still in error! If my book should contain harmful errors, then grant that it may not be spread among my rational fellow creatures, but rather be buried in eternal oblivion! My wish is merely to fulfill Your will! My wish is to promote the happiness of my fellow creatures as much as is possible for me! But should it contain useful truth, then I know for certain that You will provide for its distribution! Fill the minds of my readers who condemn this book with kind indulgence <note>original: "Nachsicht"; leniency or forbearance.</note> toward me, and prevent the opponents of my opinions from hating me myself, but rather only my opinions, if they deserve hatred! Perhaps words have slipped into this book that seem to contain mockery. But You know how much I [hate] mocking... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "Aus-" suggests the next sentence begins with "Ausspottung" (deriding/mocking) or a similar word.</note>
